This viewpoint counters the AI doomers and even the big AI labs themselves, which sometimes position their models as on the verge of consciousness (Anthropic) or as alien minds (OpenAI) . While Huang deals with the fallout of his actions, the loudest voice of this counter-narrative is, for the foreseeable future, silenced. Huang also just convinced a long list of PC makers to buy into his long-time dream of providing CPUs (the main processor chips) for them. extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.
On Thursday came reports that the ousted former CEO had an intimate relationship with a second employee.

The revelation, reported by Reuters, follows allegations of two other extramarital ⁠affairs that led to Jensen Huang’s dramatic resignation – one with Alice Huang, ​an alleged Chinese spy, and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound.

Kress wrote that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.

extraction.body: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News . Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month. The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees . Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said the testimony is expected before Thanksgiving, according to TechCrunch. Three committees are driving the request: Mast’s House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party chaired by John Moolenaar, and the House Intelligence Committee chaired by Rick Crawford. The lawmakers sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting his appearance, according to TechCrunch. Mast said the testimony will be conducted behind closed doors, with the session expected to be recorded and transcribed. CNBC reported the session will likely occur under oath , though the final date and format are still being negotiated. Mast said Huang has “very serious questions to answer” and pointed to disagreements over export controls as a specific concern, while also describing Nvidia as an important U.S. company, according to TechCrunch. That framing suggests lawmakers may examine Nvidia’s commercial interests in China alongside the national security allegations. Nvidia’s advanced chips are a primary target of U.S. efforts to restrict China’s access to AI computing infrastructure . Congressional scrutiny of Huang’s export-policy positions could inform how that policy develops going forward. U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect that Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based data-center company Megaspeed, was connected to Chinese intelligence . These remain reported allegations, not established findings. Beijing has formally rejected them, according to the BBC. Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation after reports of two alleged affairs , one involving Alice Huang. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO , and the board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The congressional session could bring three issues under examination at once: Nvidia’s leadership transition, its contacts involving China, and its role in semiconductor export policy. The available reporting does not establish that Huang or Nvidia violated U.S. law. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Nvidia has not publicly addressed the scope of its internal investigation , and no timeline for its conclusion has been reported. Huang will appear before three House committees in a closed-door, likely sworn session focused on China ties and semiconductor export policy

Senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena Jensen Huang if he refused to cooperate, and Wednesday night he agreed Wednesday night to appear before Congress. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said the testimony is expected before Thanksgiving, according to TechCrunch.

Three committees are driving the request: Mast’s House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party chaired by John Moolenaar, and the House Intelligence Committee chaired by Rick Crawford. The lawmakers sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting his appearance, according to TechCrunch.

Mast said the testimony will be conducted behind closed doors, with the session expected to be recorded and transcribed. CNBC reported the session will likely occur under oath , though the final date and format are still being negotiated.

Mast said Huang has “very serious questions to answer” and pointed to disagreements over export controls as a specific concern, while also describing Nvidia as an important U.S. company, according to TechCrunch. That framing suggests lawmakers may examine Nvidia’s commercial interests in China alongside the national security allegations.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are a primary target of U.S. efforts to restrict China’s access to AI computing infrastructure . Congressional scrutiny of Huang’s export-policy positions could inform how that policy develops going forward.

U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect that Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based data-center company Megaspeed, was connected to Chinese intelligence . These remain reported allegations, not established findings. Beijing has formally rejected them, according to the BBC.

Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation after reports of two alleged affairs , one involving Alice Huang. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO , and the board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The congressional session could bring three issues under examination at once: Nvidia’s leadership transition, its contacts involving China, and its role in semiconductor export policy. The available reporting does not establish that Huang or Nvidia violated U.S. law.

The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Nvidia has not publicly addressed the scope of its internal investigation , and no timeline for its conclusion has been reported.

sources.title: Google's latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions - TechCrunch
passages: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos.
The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.
In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly.
Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says.
Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally.
The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do.
Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries.
This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.

extraction.body: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.” While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement. The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level. In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode. In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question. Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains. The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode. Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models. The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens. On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out. In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform. Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally. sources.title: Google brings Gemini 4 Hydrogen to Search with smarter answers and better visuals - Android Authority
passages: Google Search is getting a major upgrade, and it could noticeably change how you find information online.
Google is rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen to all users worldwide, bringing smarter answers, better visuals, and a better understanding of even the most complicated questions.
One of the biggest changes is that you won’t have to be quite as careful about how you phrase your searches.
Whether you’re asking several questions at once, making a few typos, or looking for something very specific, Google says Search will be better at figuring out what you actually need.
And to make those answers more relevant, Google is also improving how Search gathers information from the web.
It can break down complicated questions into smaller searches, explore different aspects at once, and find relevant information from a wider range of websites.
That means you could find helpful sources that wouldn’t necessarily appear in your usual searches.
So, if you’re comparing two products, you could get a side-by-side breakdown of their differences instead of piecing everything together yourself.

extraction.body: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.” While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement. The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level. In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode. In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question. Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains. The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode. Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models. The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens. On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out. In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform. Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally. Google I/O is less than a day away, and the annual software showcase would be the perfect opportunity for Google and its partners to showcase their 2026 Android XR tech: the XR glasses we’ve been promised will land this year. Google isn’t a stranger to smart specs, but since the rapid rise and fall of Google Glass, we’ve seen the likes of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses take the smart specs world by storm, and now the old king wants his crown back. But with Google taking a software-centric approach — letting others handle the hardware — it makes sense that this new generation of smart glasses would land at a software show like I/O. So from Xreal and Samsung , to Gucci and Gentle Monster, here are the three smart glasses announcements we’ll hopefully see on May 19 — and why you should get excited. I love Xreal’s specs, and have done for a while — if you want a pair of XR glasses you’ll struggle to beat the Xreal One Pros . So I’m especially excited to see the final version of its Project Aura Android XR glasses, and they’re also the pair we’re most likely to find at Google I/O (because unlike Samsung, Xreal doesn’t have a high profile tech events of its own in the calendar). The big difference between Xreal’s Aura glasses and some other AI smart glasses we’ve been seeing is they’ll be wired. This matches Xreal’s XR approach with previous models and offers some design advantages, but also some constraints. With no internal battery the Project Aura glasses should feel lighter and less bulky, but they’ll need to run from a connected device (in Aura’s case that’s a dedicated compute puck that doubles as a trackpad and a battery pack) plus they’ll be best suited to stationary activities (working, and watching TV) rather than using them on the move. This approach might not be as mobile as the Ray-Ban and Samsung AI or AR specs, but should be a lot more capable where it counts.The glasses virtually project a giant display in front of your face, like your own private cinema, and boast the same superb optics as the Xreal One (so expect excellent OLED contrast and colors, a wide field of view, and fewer disruptive reflections in the lenses compared with rivals on the market). Whether you want a virtual display for working across multiple windows at once, or an immersive portable cinema for your face the Xreal One pro are the glasses to get because of these optics. Where Aura improves on the current design is it includes cameras by default for hand and object tracking. It's a bit more basic than the Samsung Galaxy XR headset's system as Xreal lacks eye tracking, but it should make your Android XR experiences feel more interactive than Xreal's previous tech. The issue is I expect these specs will be pricey. The Xreal One Pros launched at $649, with a camera Xreal Eye add-on costing $99. The puck is also reminiscent of the Beam Pro and is likely to add a couple hundred to the price meaning we might be lucky if Xreal's Aura comes in under $1,000. Even though I believe Samsung will focus on its own launch event — perhaps tying its smart glasses release into its annual foldables event, which typically takes place in a few months — there’s a chance it’ll instead debut its glasses at I/O. Not just one pair at that, we might get to see two. The first would be a more standard AI-focused design with a camera, speakers, and microphones, but no display, just like the basic (but impressive) Ray-Ban Meta specs. Speaking of, the design recently leaked, and they do look strikingly similar to the Ray-Ban model. The only difference we know so far is they'll rely on Gemini instead of Meta AI, which is generally agreed to be a more capable assistant, and has better interoperability between the core Android apps for more personalized contextual responses. Based on my experience with Ray-Ban smart glasses, AI assistance can be super handy, especially as a tourist. With a better understanding of my schedule through my calendar, or the context of the photos I've taken with my phone, I'm hoping the Gemini-powered specs might offer better day-to-day usefulness. Best of all, Samsung’s specs should be fairly affordable too. These smart glasses are rumored to cost between $379 and $499, which puts them roughly inline with Meta's pricing — though we’ll have to wait and see what Samsung announces to know for sure, pricing has been all over thanks to various global economic challenges. As for Samsung’s second pair of specs, they would be practically the same, but with a display. Now, leaks and rumors suggest the display model won’t actually land until 2027 but I expect they'll get some time in the spotlight if the displayless specs are shown off — in part to build excitement and prove Android XR has a long term plan (to rebut fears this is Google Glass 2.0), and in part to make Samsung not appear too far behind Meta’s technology (as its Ray-ban Display specs are already available to buy in the US). It's frustrating that we might have to wait a little longer for these display glasses, though, seeing the supply issues Meta has had with its version, and the high price tag, Samsung's delay might mean it can bring us a more reliably available and affordable version of this exciting emerging tech. Lastly, my bold Google I/O prediction: we’ll get an XR fashion show with models strutting down the runway in Gucci, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker smart specs. Much like how Meta has partnered with EssilorLuxottica’s Oakley and Ray-Ban, Android XR companies are partnering with fashion brands to bring some style to their specs. Given how much glasses can play into someone’s visual identity, a fashion focus is key, and offering a variety of looks is key to capturing different users and use cases — just look at Meta, its Ray-Bans are superb for everyday wear and casual vacationing, while its Oakleys are perfect for athletes. With a wider variety of brands and, hopefully, styles under its belt, Android XR seems to have an advantage over Meta again, and a fashion show moment would be the perfect way to highlight the variety it’s set to offer. Plus, Google has shown it isn’t afraid to mix things up with its events — last year, the Made by Google Pixel 10 launch show was hosted by Jimmy Fallon and featured a large cast of celebrities and segments that felt more like a variety show than a technology keynote. So I’m hoping we might see some fun smart-glasses showcases, though I’ll admit my fashion-show pitch might be a little out there — and it assumes Google, Gentle Monster, Gucci, and Warby Parker are even ready to showcase their designs. Google just announced Android XR , with a Samsung-produced headset being the first product to run the new platform. The company also confirmed that smart glasses were coming later , and we now have a better idea of how these glasses will work. Wired was able to go hands-on with a pair of prototype glasses running Android XR. The outlet confirmed that several different types of smart glasses were shown off, such as conventional spectacles and sunglasses. You could also get prescription lenses for them, as you’d expect. What about the design itself? Well, the website noted that the arms were thick, but in line with the Meta Ray-Ban Wayfarers. These prototype glasses also have a camera built into the frame complete with an LED that turns on when you’re shooting. Most of the processing is handled by a paired smartphone, and Google is apparently aiming for ” all-day” battery life as a result. It’s unclear how many features will be available without a paired phone. Nevertheless, the glasses used during the demonstration had a display, and the outlet said there “might” be options such as no display but with Gemini support, a monocular display on one lens, or a full-blown binocular display. Fingers crossed that we see options without a display as that would likely be much cheaper and offer better battery life. You simply need to tap the side of the spectacles’ frame to show the date, time, and weather. Wired tried one demo that showed turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps on the display. Looking down while using this feature revealed a wider view of your route. You can summon and pause Gemini by tapping the arm, allowing you to ask general questions about what you’re seeing. You can also get translations overlaid onto real-world text (e.g. a sign in Spanish), while the chatbot will translate spoken language for you as well. Wired added that these glasses also offer captions for real-world speech, noting that they’re not perfect but good enough for following a conversation. This certainly seems like a handy addition for accessibility purposes. Today’s phones and chatbots offer summarization smarts too, and the outlet claimed Gemini was indeed able to summarize the page of a real-world book with “shocking speed.” A video Google showed off yesterday revealed that Gemini on Android XR smart glasses can remember things, such as where you left a specific object. You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.” Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices—Google Pixel phones, Samsung Galaxy phones, and iPhones—and only select models.

That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “Glasshole”).

extraction.body: The “Intelligent Eyewear” is a collaboration between the two tech companies, with Samsung providing its hardware expertise and Google handling much of the software platform. Smart glasses are just one part of Android XR—there are also mixed-reality headsets and glasses for more immersive experiences, like last year's Samsung Galaxy XR and the upcoming Xreal Aura. Eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are heavily involved in the new smart glasses, responsible for the design and fit, similar to how Meta tapped Ray-Ban for its competing—and market-leading—wearables. Google and Samsung are leveraging Warby Parker and Gentle Monster's brick-and-mortar presence and retail expertise, which lets people demo the glasses before buying them. (Kering Eyewear, which owns brands like Lindberg and Maui Jim, has also signed up to make glasses for Android XR in the future.) The first models are available for preorder now, with official sales starting on December 10. Warby Parker's frames start at $395 and come in three styles—Alden, Reid, and Wren—as optical or sunglasses, with various prescription, lens, and width options. Gentle Monster's glasses start at $449 and come in six designs, various colors, and tints, with prescription options for most frames. The glasses weigh around 41 grams (10 grams less than Meta's new Gen 3 glasses), have a nine-hour battery life, and include a charging case that can recharge the glasses up to seven times. A touch-sensitive temple piece lets you tap to activate the onboard Gemini assistant, or slide two fingers back and forth to control the volume of the audio coming out of the glasses' speaker. They are the first devices to support the “Hey Gemini” hotword, though you can use the well-known “Hey Google” hotword if you'd like. Still, the new spoken wake phrase distinguishes the glasses as Gemini's “optimal form,” according to Juston Payne, Google's senior director of product management for XR. “We felt that these are a Gemini-forward device,” Payne tells WIRED. You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.” Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices—Google Pixel phones, Samsung Galaxy phones, and iPhones—and only select models. You'll need a Pixel 7 or newer, Galaxy S or Z Fold running Samsung's One UI 9.0 or higher, and the iPhone 13 Pro or newer. A Google spokesperson tells WIRED the company will share more about how it plans to expand support to other phones in 2027 after launch. Since you'll be buying the glasses from an eyewear brand, they will be the customer-facing party to handle any problems you may have with the device or prescriptions. Google has already previewed Intelligent Eyewear glasses with displays built into the lenses—useful for showing navigation instructions or real-time captions for folks with hearing issues. However, they are not ready yet; Payne says they're currently being tested by “non-Googlers” and are still on the road map, though he didn't share a specific release window. As for plans to launch audio-only smart glasses, like Meta's recent Ray-Ban Audio, Warby Parker co-CEO Dave Gilboa tells WIRED, “There's a pretty robust pipeline of additional products.” What Can They Do? Smart glasses have been around for a few years, but they come in many forms. Unlike display smart glasses designed to plug into a laptop to mirror or extend your screen, or more immersive glasses like Meta's VR Glasses, which layer virtual experiences over the real world, Intelligent Eyewear is more akin to what Google pitched years ago with the original Google Glass. You can listen to music, take phone calls, and get audio navigation through Google Maps. Yes, you can snap photos and videos too, though Payne quickly notes that these glasses are designed more to have Gemini assist you throughout the day than to capture content. That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “Glasshole”). “We learned through Glass that you can make people uncomfortable if you're not clearly communicating,” Payne says. To that end, Google is announcing a series of policies and features alongside the glasses to assuage concerns. When you ask Gemini to look at something, those visuals are not saved in your Gemini History, and Google says it will not use them to train AI models or target ads. The glasses will automatically redact the faces of people around you before Gemini processes the visual data. We've highlighted all of Google's privacy-focused announcements around its glasses in a separate story. Most of the features that Google is positioning around Intelligent Eyewear rely on Gemini. And if you use Samsung Notes on a Samsung phone, it'll know that's where you likely want your notes saved. A swipe back on the glasses' arm will end the interaction. Speaking of, early next year, Google says users can use gestures on devices like the Fitbit Air or Google Pixel Watch to control music playback or activate Gemini on the glasses right from their wrist. Google is also collaborating with Aira so you can stream the glasses' feed straight to a human interpreter for real-time visual support. To help demystify these features—and convince consumers that smart glasses aren't just a fad for tech bros—Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are both launching pop-up experiences in New York City this week. Gentle Monster's pop-up will run for about a month, but Warby Parker's “Literatureland” will be open through 2027, letting people walk through the experience with a pair of nonprescription glasses to demo Gemini's capabilities. “These are the original wearables that have been around for hundreds of years,” Warby Parker's Gilboa says.

extraction.body: The Xreal Aura, spatial computing glasses made in partnership with Google for the Android XR platform, are now available to order. We first learned about these XR glasses at Google I/O 2026, and early adopters can finally try them in a matter of weeks. The futuristic XR device combines elements of augmented reality and virtual reality in a pair of smart glasses. They're the first wired smart glasses to run on the new Android XR operating system from Google. The glasses and accessories are available for preorder at the Xreal website as of today, and they're scheduled to ship in mid-November, according to a press release shared with Mashable. Customers who preorder the glasses can save $180 on the hefty $1,279 price tag.“Xreal Aura is finally here, and we're so proud to unlock new ways for people to work, watch, play, and build," said Chi Xu, co-founder and CEO of XREAL, in a press release.The Xreal Aura utilizes dual Sony Micro-OLED displays to create a virtual display with a 70-degree field of view, up to 1,050 nits of brightness, and up to a 120Hz refresh rate. Credit: Xreal Credit: Xreal Xreal is one of the leading augmented reality companies, known for its tethered AR glasses, which project a large virtual display into the user's field of view. The Xreal Aura will provide spatial computing and virtual reality experiences usually associated with headsets in the smart glasses form factor.The Xreal Aura is part of a new generation of spatial computing smart glasses, along with the Specs AR glasses from Snap and the recently announced Meta VR glasses. The Meta VR glasses have a $1,299 price tag but won't launch until spring 2027.What do the Xreal Aura Glasses do? Credit: Xreal / Mashable Photo Composite Xreal says the new glasses will support "productivity, immersive entertainment, and next-generation XR experiences."The Xreal Aura offer the same augmented reality features as other AR smart glasses, but they up the ante with spatial computing experiences powered by the Android XR operating system and Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform. (A press release states that the glasses were made in partnership with Google and Qualcomm.) Unlike most AR glasses, the Xreal Aura can also be controlled via voice and hand movements, thanks to onboard sensors and cameras. Instead of simply plugging into a user's smartphone, laptop, or gaming device, the Aura glasses come with a puck, which houses the battery and powers most of the compute necessary for spatial computing.The Apple Vision Pro introduced spatial computing into the public consciousness. The technology turns a user's surroundings into a 360-degree virtual canvas, and users can open apps, games, entertainment, and AI tools directly into their space. However, unlike headsets, which can be extremely limiting, smart glasses don't limit a user's movements or block their peripheral vision. “This is a defining moment for XR," Xu said in a press release. "We built AURA for people who want the power of spatial computing without being removed from the world around them. With transparent lenses, a category-leading lightweight design, Gemini by your side, and access to the Android ecosystem from day-one, the promise of XR is more approachable than ever."The Xreal Aura will also offer support for Gemini, letting users ask questions about their environment or complete tasks across apps.Spatial photos, virtual reality, and more Credit: Xreal / Android XR Using Google Photos and Android XR, Aura users will be able to view their photos and videos in new immersive ways. Via Google Maps, users can explore destinations in immersive 3D, either with an aerial view or via Street View.Users can also enjoy 360-degree and VR180 video content on YouTube.New XR experiencesAt launch, users will also be able to access a library of more than 150 XR experiences, with more to come in the months ahead. We first learned about these XR glasses at Google I/O 2026, and early adopters can finally try them in a matter of weeks.
The futuristic XR device combines elements of augmented reality and virtual reality in a pair of smart glasses.
They're the first wired smart glasses to run on the new Android XR operating system from Google.
The glasses and accessories are available for preorder at the Xreal website as of today, and they're scheduled to ship in mid-November, according to a press release shared with Mashable.

Customers who preorder the glasses can save $180 on the hefty $1,279 price tag.“Xreal Aura is finally here, and we're so proud to unlock new ways for people to work, watch, play, and build," said Chi Xu, co-founder and CEO of XREAL, in a press release.The Xreal Aura utilizes dual Sony Micro-OLED displays to create a virtual display with a 70-degree field of view, up to 1,050 nits of brightness, and up to a 120Hz refresh rate.
Credit: Xreal Credit: Xreal Xreal is one of the leading augmented reality companies, known for its tethered AR glasses, which project a large virtual display into the user's field of view.

The Xreal Aura will provide spatial computing and virtual reality experiences usually associated with headsets in the smart glasses form factor.The Xreal Aura is part of a new generation of spatial computing smart glasses, along with the Specs AR glasses from Snap and the recently announced Meta VR glasses.
The Meta VR glasses have a $1,299 price tag but won't launch until spring 2027.What do the Xreal Aura Glasses do?

Credit: Xreal / Mashable Photo Composite Xreal says the new glasses will support "productivity, immersive entertainment, and next-generation XR experiences."The Xreal Aura offer the same augmented reality features as other AR smart glasses, but they up the ante with spatial computing experiences powered by the Android XR operating system and Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform. (A press release states that the glasses were made in partnership with Google and Qualcomm.) Unlike most AR glasses, the Xreal Aura can also be controlled via voice and hand movements, thanks to onboard sensors and cameras.

Instead of simply plugging into a user's smartphone, laptop, or gaming device, the Aura glasses come with a puck, which houses the battery and powers most of the compute necessary for spatial computing.The Apple Vision Pro introduced spatial computing into the public consciousness.
The technology turns a user's surroundings into a 360-degree virtual canvas, and users can open apps, games, entertainment, and AI tools directly into their space.

However, unlike headsets, which can be extremely limiting, smart glasses don't limit a user's movements or block their peripheral vision. “This is a defining moment for XR," Xu said in a press release.
"We built AURA for people who want the power of spatial computing without being removed from the world around them.

With transparent lenses, a category-leading lightweight design, Gemini by your side, and access to the Android ecosystem from day-one, the promise of XR is more approachable than ever."The Xreal Aura will also offer support for Gemini, letting users ask questions about their environment or complete tasks across apps.Spatial photos, virtual reality, and more Credit: Xreal / Android XR Using Google Photos and Android XR, Aura users will be able to view their photos and videos in new immersive ways.

Via Google Maps, users can explore destinations in immersive 3D, either with an aerial view or via Street View.Users can also enjoy 360-degree and VR180 video content on YouTube.New XR experiencesAt launch, users will also be able to access a library of more than 150 XR experiences, with more to come in the months ahead.

Some of the highlights include:NBA App for Android XRFallout: Factions video gameProject Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, a mixed-reality adventure NASCAR XR appOh My Galaxy!, a physics-based arcade gameXR HoloMedicineSimply Piano XRWhere to preorder the Xreal AuraThe Xreal Aura are available for preorder now exclusively at the Xreal online store.
The glasses have a retail price of $1,279 but are available for $1,099 for a limited time.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google I/O is less than a day away, and the annual software showcase would be the perfect opportunity for Google and its partners to showcase their 2026 Android XR tech: the XR glasses we’ve been promised will land this year.
So from Xreal and Samsung , to Gucci and Gentle Monster, here are the three smart glasses announcements we’ll hopefully see on May 19 — and why you should get excited.
I love Xreal’s specs, and have done for a while — if you want a pair of XR glasses you’ll struggle to beat the Xreal One Pros .

Now, leaks and rumors suggest the display model won’t actually land until 2027 but I expect they'll get some time in the spotlight if the displayless specs are shown off — in part to build excitement and prove Android XR has a long term plan (to rebut fears this is Google Glass 2.0), and in part to make Samsung not appear too far behind Meta’s technology (as its Ray-ban Display specs are already available to buy in the US).
But with Google taking a software-centric approach — letting others handle the hardware — it makes sense that this new generation of smart glasses would land at a software show like I/O.
Based on my experience with Ray-Ban smart glasses, AI assistance can be super handy, especially as a tourist.
Where Aura improves on the current design is it includes cameras by default for hand and object tracking.
It's a bit more basic than the Samsung Galaxy XR headset's system as Xreal lacks eye tracking, but it should make your Android XR experiences feel more interactive than Xreal's previous tech.

Google I/O is less than a day away, and the annual software showcase would be the perfect opportunity for Google and its partners to showcase their 2026 Android XR tech: the XR glasses we’ve been promised will land this year. Google isn’t a stranger to smart specs, but since the rapid rise and fall of Google Glass, we’ve seen the likes of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses take the smart specs world by storm, and now the old king wants his crown back. But with Google taking a software-centric approach — letting others handle the hardware — it makes sense that this new generation of smart glasses would land at a software show like I/O. So from Xreal and Samsung , to Gucci and Gentle Monster, here are the three smart glasses announcements we’ll hopefully see on May 19 — and why you should get excited. I love Xreal’s specs, and have done for a while — if you want a pair of XR glasses you’ll struggle to beat the Xreal One Pros . So I’m especially excited to see the final version of its Project Aura Android XR glasses, and they’re also the pair we’re most likely to find at Google I/O (because unlike Samsung, Xreal doesn’t have a high profile tech events of its own in the calendar). The big difference between Xreal’s Aura glasses and some other AI smart glasses we’ve been seeing is they’ll be wired. This matches Xreal’s XR approach with previous models and offers some design advantages, but also some constraints. With no internal battery the Project Aura glasses should feel lighter and less bulky, but they’ll need to run from a connected device (in Aura’s case that’s a dedicated compute puck that doubles as a trackpad and a battery pack) plus they’ll be best suited to stationary activities (working, and watching TV) rather than using them on the move. This approach might not be as mobile as the Ray-Ban and Samsung AI or AR specs, but should be a lot more capable where it counts.The glasses virtually project a giant display in front of your face, like your own private cinema, and boast the same superb optics as the Xreal One (so expect excellent OLED contrast and colors, a wide field of view, and fewer disruptive reflections in the lenses compared with rivals on the market). Whether you want a virtual display for working across multiple windows at once, or an immersive portable cinema for your face the Xreal One pro are the glasses to get because of these optics. Where Aura improves on the current design is it includes cameras by default for hand and object tracking. It's a bit more basic than the Samsung Galaxy XR headset's system as Xreal lacks eye tracking, but it should make your Android XR experiences feel more interactive than Xreal's previous tech. The issue is I expect these specs will be pricey. The Xreal One Pros launched at $649, with a camera Xreal Eye add-on costing $99. The puck is also reminiscent of the Beam Pro and is likely to add a couple hundred to the price meaning we might be lucky if Xreal's Aura comes in under $1,000. Even though I believe Samsung will focus on its own launch event — perhaps tying its smart glasses release into its annual foldables event, which typically takes place in a few months — there’s a chance it’ll instead debut its glasses at I/O. Not just one pair at that, we might get to see two. The first would be a more standard AI-focused design with a camera, speakers, and microphones, but no display, just like the basic (but impressive) Ray-Ban Meta specs. Speaking of, the design recently leaked, and they do look strikingly similar to the Ray-Ban model. The only difference we know so far is they'll rely on Gemini instead of Meta AI, which is generally agreed to be a more capable assistant, and has better interoperability between the core Android apps for more personalized contextual responses. Based on my experience with Ray-Ban smart glasses, AI assistance can be super handy, especially as a tourist. With a better understanding of my schedule through my calendar, or the context of the photos I've taken with my phone, I'm hoping the Gemini-powered specs might offer better day-to-day usefulness. Best of all, Samsung’s specs should be fairly affordable too. These smart glasses are rumored to cost between $379 and $499, which puts them roughly inline with Meta's pricing — though we’ll have to wait and see what Samsung announces to know for sure, pricing has been all over thanks to various global economic challenges. As for Samsung’s second pair of specs, they would be practically the same, but with a display. Now, leaks and rumors suggest the display model won’t actually land until 2027 but I expect they'll get some time in the spotlight if the displayless specs are shown off — in part to build excitement and prove Android XR has a long term plan (to rebut fears this is Google Glass 2.0), and in part to make Samsung not appear too far behind Meta’s technology (as its Ray-ban Display specs are already available to buy in the US). It's frustrating that we might have to wait a little longer for these display glasses, though, seeing the supply issues Meta has had with its version, and the high price tag, Samsung's delay might mean it can bring us a more reliably available and affordable version of this exciting emerging tech. Lastly, my bold Google I/O prediction: we’ll get an XR fashion show with models strutting down the runway in Gucci, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker smart specs. Much like how Meta has partnered with EssilorLuxottica’s Oakley and Ray-Ban, Android XR companies are partnering with fashion brands to bring some style to their specs. Given how much glasses can play into someone’s visual identity, a fashion focus is key, and offering a variety of looks is key to capturing different users and use cases — just look at Meta, its Ray-Bans are superb for everyday wear and casual vacationing, while its Oakleys are perfect for athletes. With a wider variety of brands and, hopefully, styles under its belt, Android XR seems to have an advantage over Meta again, and a fashion show moment would be the perfect way to highlight the variety it’s set to offer. Plus, Google has shown it isn’t afraid to mix things up with its events — last year, the Made by Google Pixel 10 launch show was hosted by Jimmy Fallon and featured a large cast of celebrities and segments that felt more like a variety show than a technology keynote. So I’m hoping we might see some fun smart-glasses showcases, though I’ll admit my fashion-show pitch might be a little out there — and it assumes Google, Gentle Monster, Gucci, and Warby Parker are even ready to showcase their designs. The first models are available for preorder now, with official sales starting on December 10.
The “Intelligent Eyewear” is a collaboration between the two tech companies, with Samsung providing its hardware expertise and Google handling much of the software platform.
You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.” Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices—Google Pixel phones, Samsung Galaxy phones, and iPhones—and only select models.
Still, the new spoken wake phrase distinguishes the glasses as Gemini's “optimal form,” according to Juston Payne, Google's senior director of product management for XR.
You'll need a Pixel 7 or newer, Galaxy S or Z Fold running Samsung's One UI 9.0 or higher, and the iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

As for plans to launch audio-only smart glasses, like Meta's recent Ray-Ban Audio, Warby Parker co-CEO Dave Gilboa tells WIRED, “There's a pretty robust pipeline of additional products.” What Can They Do?

That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “Glasshole”).
Google has already previewed Intelligent Eyewear glasses with displays built into the lenses—useful for showing navigation instructions or real-time captions for folks with hearing issues.
To that end, Google is announcing a series of policies and features alongside the glasses to assuage concerns.
We've highlighted all of Google's privacy-focused announcements around its glasses in a separate story.

Speaking of, early next year, Google says users can use gestures on devices like the Fitbit Air or Google Pixel Watch to control music playback or activate Gemini on the glasses right from their wrist.
Smart glasses have been around for a few years, but they come in many forms.
When you ask Gemini to look at something, those visuals are not saved in your Gemini History, and Google says it will not use them to train AI models or target ads.
And if you use Samsung Notes on a Samsung phone, it'll know that's where you likely want your notes saved.

extraction.body: The “Intelligent Eyewear” is a collaboration between the two tech companies, with Samsung providing its hardware expertise and Google handling much of the software platform. Smart glasses are just one part of Android XR—there are also mixed-reality headsets and glasses for more immersive experiences, like last year's Samsung Galaxy XR and the upcoming Xreal Aura. Eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are heavily involved in the new smart glasses, responsible for the design and fit, similar to how Meta tapped Ray-Ban for its competing—and market-leading—wearables. Google and Samsung are leveraging Warby Parker and Gentle Monster's brick-and-mortar presence and retail expertise, which lets people demo the glasses before buying them. (Kering Eyewear, which owns brands like Lindberg and Maui Jim, has also signed up to make glasses for Android XR in the future.) The first models are available for preorder now, with official sales starting on December 10. Warby Parker's frames start at $395 and come in three styles—Alden, Reid, and Wren—as optical or sunglasses, with various prescription, lens, and width options. Gentle Monster's glasses start at $449 and come in six designs, various colors, and tints, with prescription options for most frames. The glasses weigh around 41 grams (10 grams less than Meta's new Gen 3 glasses), have a nine-hour battery life, and include a charging case that can recharge the glasses up to seven times. A touch-sensitive temple piece lets you tap to activate the onboard Gemini assistant, or slide two fingers back and forth to control the volume of the audio coming out of the glasses' speaker. They are the first devices to support the “Hey Gemini” hotword, though you can use the well-known “Hey Google” hotword if you'd like. Still, the new spoken wake phrase distinguishes the glasses as Gemini's “optimal form,” according to Juston Payne, Google's senior director of product management for XR. “We felt that these are a Gemini-forward device,” Payne tells WIRED. You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.” Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices—Google Pixel phones, Samsung Galaxy phones, and iPhones—and only select models. You'll need a Pixel 7 or newer, Galaxy S or Z Fold running Samsung's One UI 9.0 or higher, and the iPhone 13 Pro or newer. A Google spokesperson tells WIRED the company will share more about how it plans to expand support to other phones in 2027 after launch. Since you'll be buying the glasses from an eyewear brand, they will be the customer-facing party to handle any problems you may have with the device or prescriptions. Google has already previewed Intelligent Eyewear glasses with displays built into the lenses—useful for showing navigation instructions or real-time captions for folks with hearing issues. However, they are not ready yet; Payne says they're currently being tested by “non-Googlers” and are still on the road map, though he didn't share a specific release window. As for plans to launch audio-only smart glasses, like Meta's recent Ray-Ban Audio, Warby Parker co-CEO Dave Gilboa tells WIRED, “There's a pretty robust pipeline of additional products.” What Can They Do? Smart glasses have been around for a few years, but they come in many forms. Unlike display smart glasses designed to plug into a laptop to mirror or extend your screen, or more immersive glasses like Meta's VR Glasses, which layer virtual experiences over the real world, Intelligent Eyewear is more akin to what Google pitched years ago with the original Google Glass. You can listen to music, take phone calls, and get audio navigation through Google Maps. Yes, you can snap photos and videos too, though Payne quickly notes that these glasses are designed more to have Gemini assist you throughout the day than to capture content. That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “Glasshole”). “We learned through Glass that you can make people uncomfortable if you're not clearly communicating,” Payne says. To that end, Google is announcing a series of policies and features alongside the glasses to assuage concerns. When you ask Gemini to look at something, those visuals are not saved in your Gemini History, and Google says it will not use them to train AI models or target ads. The glasses will automatically redact the faces of people around you before Gemini processes the visual data. We've highlighted all of Google's privacy-focused announcements around its glasses in a separate story. Most of the features that Google is positioning around Intelligent Eyewear rely on Gemini. And if you use Samsung Notes on a Samsung phone, it'll know that's where you likely want your notes saved. A swipe back on the glasses' arm will end the interaction. Speaking of, early next year, Google says users can use gestures on devices like the Fitbit Air or Google Pixel Watch to control music playback or activate Gemini on the glasses right from their wrist. Google is also collaborating with Aira so you can stream the glasses' feed straight to a human interpreter for real-time visual support. To help demystify these features—and convince consumers that smart glasses aren't just a fad for tech bros—Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are both launching pop-up experiences in New York City this week. Gentle Monster's pop-up will run for about a month, but Warby Parker's “Literatureland” will be open through 2027, letting people walk through the experience with a pair of nonprescription glasses to demo Gemini's capabilities. “These are the original wearables that have been around for hundreds of years,” Warby Parker's Gilboa says.

Jensen Huang's "I made it" moment never translated to long weekends and a step back from day-to-day operations. Despite Nvidia becoming the world's most valuable company, its CEO Huang just admitted he still operates on a mix of fear, anxiety, and even going bankrupt. "You know the phrase '30 days from going out of business,' I've used for 33 years," Huang said on an episode of The Joe Rogan Experienc e . "But the feeling doesn't change. The sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity—it doesn't leave you." Nvidia has made itself one of the clear leaders in the AI race. What started as a graphics card producer grew into a tech powerhouse, building chips, systems, and software that power most large AI models in cloud data centers around the world. Last month, Nvidia became the first public company to reach a market capitalization of $5 trillion . Yet Huang still can't shake the feeling that the company could vanish overnight. "It is exhausting," he said, while adding that he's "always in a state of anxiety." The veteran CEO revealed he still works seven days a week, every moment he is awake to ensure his nightmare doesn't become—including checking his emails from 4 a.m.: "Every day. Every single day. Not one day missed. Including Thanksgiving, Christmas." Huang recounted an incident of a near collapse in the mid-1990s, when the company realized its first graphics technology was flawed just as it was developing a chip for Sega's next game console. With money running out, he flew to Japan to tell Sega's CEO the product wouldn't work and that they should cancel the deal, yet he also admitted Nvidia needed the final $5 million payment to stay afloat. Sega converted the remaining funds into an investment, giving the struggling startup the lifeline it needed to stay alive. "Suffering is part of the journey. You will appreciate it for these horrible feelings that you have when things are not going so well. You will appreciate it so much more when they do go well," he added. Huang previously wished Stanford students " ample doses of pain and suffering ". In his eyes, adversity is key to having resilience, low expectations and ultimately success. Even now, the fear of failure is still Huang's greatest motivator. "I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed," he said on the podcast. "Failure drives me more than greed or whatever it is." Huang isn't the only one to be born with the "work gene" in his family. Both of his kids work every day, too. Madison and Spencer, both in their 30s, started the company as interns in 2020 and 2022. "My kids work every day. Both of my kids work at Nvidia. They work every day," Huang said. Before that, both didn't show much interest in working for the company after high school. Madison attended the Culinary Institute of America , with her brother Spencer studying marketing in Chicago, then moving to Taiwan to study Mandarin, while doing so, he opened up a cocktail bar in Taipei. "Now we have three people working every day and they want to work with me every day and so it's a lot of work," Huang said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

That approach persisted, as recently as this week.

"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday.
"How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."
Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S.

He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term.
Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.

Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer."
"I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC.

In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects.
That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.
Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

extraction.body: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market." When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it. One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated. Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday.
