extraction.body: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake. On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government. But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go. The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list. Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him? Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed , writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built. It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign. Erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote . “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.” U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang. Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.” Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat. For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform. That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.” Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them. The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services. Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.” In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance , which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions. The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang. OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban. The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027. That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence —arguably, the most powerful company on earth. Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote , praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company. Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote . He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI. Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X . “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.” If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right. Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.” Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy. In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts. Bitcoin and privacy advocate Neil Woodfine described Huang as a founder who had built Nvidia to the pinnacle and championed free, local AI, only to be displaced by a managerial establishment convinced it could do better. This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern… — Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026 Not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit , warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. The concern from Washington has been largely uniform: the possibility of compromising pressure against the leader of a company central to U.S. AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has remained supportive of Huang: “He’s definitely suffering,” he told the press. “I think he’ll be in good shape.” Speculation about Huang’s next job spread just as quickly as criticism of his last one. Responding to an X user asking him to hire Huang, Elon Musk replied , “That would be an honor.”

Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.”

Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat.

For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform.

That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.”

Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them.
The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services.

Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.”

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance , which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions.

The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang.
OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban.

The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.
That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence —arguably, the most powerful company on earth.

Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote , praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company.

Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote . He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI.

Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X . “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.”
If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.

Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.”

Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy.
In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts.

Bitcoin and privacy advocate Neil Woodfine described Huang as a founder who had built Nvidia to the pinnacle and championed free, local AI, only to be displaced by a managerial establishment convinced it could do better.

This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern…
— Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026

Despite Nvidia becoming the world's most valuable company, its CEO Huang just admitted he still operates on a mix of fear, anxiety, and even going bankrupt.

"You know the phrase '30 days from going out of business,' I've used for 33 years," Huang said on an episode of The Joe Rogan Experienc e . "But the feeling doesn't change. The sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity—it doesn't leave you."

Nvidia has made itself one of the clear leaders in the AI race. What started as a graphics card producer grew into a tech powerhouse, building chips, systems, and software that power most large AI models in cloud data centers around the world. Last month, Nvidia became the first public company to reach a market capitalization of $5 trillion . Yet Huang still can't shake the feeling that the company could vanish overnight.
"It is exhausting," he said, while adding that he's "always in a state of anxiety."

The veteran CEO revealed he still works seven days a week, every moment he is awake to ensure his nightmare doesn't become—including checking his emails from 4 a.m.: "Every day. Every single day. Not one day missed. Including Thanksgiving, Christmas."
Huang recounted an incident of a near collapse in the mid-1990s, when the company realized its first graphics technology was flawed just as it was developing a chip for Sega's next game console.

With money running out, he flew to Japan to tell Sega's CEO the product wouldn't work and that they should cancel the deal, yet he also admitted Nvidia needed the final $5 million payment to stay afloat. Sega converted the remaining funds into an investment, giving the struggling startup the lifeline it needed to stay alive.

"Suffering is part of the journey. You will appreciate it for these horrible feelings that you have when things are not going so well. You will appreciate it so much more when they do go well," he added.
Huang previously wished Stanford students " ample doses of pain and suffering ". In his eyes, adversity is key to having resilience, low expectations and ultimately success.
Even now, the fear of failure is still Huang's greatest motivator.
"I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed," he said on the podcast. "Failure drives me more than greed or whatever it is."
Huang isn't the only one to be born with the "work gene" in his family. Both of his kids work every day, too. Madison and Spencer, both in their 30s, started the company as interns in 2020 and 2022.
"My kids work every day. Both of my kids work at Nvidia. They work every day," Huang said.

Before that, both didn't show much interest in working for the company after high school. Madison attended the Culinary Institute of America , with her brother Spencer studying marketing in Chicago, then moving to Taiwan to study Mandarin, while doing so, he opened up a cocktail bar in Taipei.
"Now we have three people working every day and they want to work with me every day and so it's a lot of work," Huang said.
This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

extraction.body: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market." When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it. One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated. Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son. On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said. Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times. Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer." "I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC. That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks. Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution.

Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman.
Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."

It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.

Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games.

Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.

In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps.

Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google.

Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private.
In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world.

"He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market."

When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it.

One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated.

Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.

The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China.
U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday.

"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."

But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son.

On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said.
Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.

Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer."
"I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC.

That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks.
Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

passages: The situation surrounding Huang has unfolded quickly, with The New York Times only reporting on Friday that Huang and the suspected spy were “close” before other dominoes started to fall, leading to a swift fall from grace for one of the biggest names in technology. Prominent voices in technology have come out in support of Huang, with some calling the resignation a “waste” and a sad day for “all humanity.” The narrative among those leaders on X, at least, is that Huang’s resignation was rushed — perhaps an overreaction to salacious news stories about his personal life.

extraction.body: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake. On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government. But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go. The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list. Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him? Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed , writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built. It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign. Erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote . “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.” U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang. Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.” Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat. For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform. That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.” Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them. The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services. Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.” In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance , which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions. The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang. OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban. The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027. That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence —arguably, the most powerful company on earth. Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote , praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company. Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote . He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI. Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X . “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.” If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right. Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.” Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy. In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts. Bitcoin and privacy advocate Neil Woodfine described Huang as a founder who had built Nvidia to the pinnacle and championed free, local AI, only to be displaced by a managerial establishment convinced it could do better. This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern… — Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026 Not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit , warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. The concern from Washington has been largely uniform: the possibility of compromising pressure against the leader of a company central to U.S. AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has remained supportive of Huang: “He’s definitely suffering,” he told the press. “I think he’ll be in good shape.” Speculation about Huang’s next job spread just as quickly as criticism of his last one. Responding to an X user asking him to hire Huang, Elon Musk replied , “That would be an honor.”

extraction.body: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market." When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it. One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated. Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son. On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said. Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times. Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer." "I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC. That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks. Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

Jensen Huang resigned immediately as president, chief executive officer, and board member of Nvidia on Nov. 12, 2026 , the company confirmed in an official press release. Colette Kress , Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, was named interim CEO effective the same day. Kress will hold two of Nvidia's most critical roles at once while the board identifies a permanent successor. Kress will carry both the CFO and interim CEO roles simultaneously while Nvidia's board conducts a search for a permanent successor, according to the company's investor relations announcement. The board said it will consider both internal and external candidates. Huang's departure removes the AI-chip industry's most prominent executive voice and leaves open questions about Nvidia's strategic direction. Huang co-founded Nvidia and ran it for more than three decades, building it into a roughly $4 trillion company, according to contemporaneous reporting. His departure raises immediate questions about who carries Nvidia's voice on export policy, open-source AI access, and Washington relationships. Nvidia's stock had risen approximately fourteenfold since ChatGPT's late-2022 debut. A recent pullback, tied to broader AI-share weakness and the controversy surrounding Huang, has since trimmed that run. Board Chair Harvey Jones moved quickly to address concerns about continuity in operations and customer commitments. Jones said the board had "full confidence" in Kress and the leadership team and expected operations, customer commitments, and the product roadmap to continue without interruption, according to CNBC's live coverage. Nvidia's official announcement reinforced that message, stating no interruption to its product roadmap was expected. Nvidia's official announcement does not state a reason for Huang's departure; details of the surrounding investigation come primarily from reporting by The New York Times. The New York Times reported that Huang acknowledged a personal relationship with Alice Huang, a business executive associated with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. The Times separately reported that U.S. intelligence agencies concluded Alice Huang was connected to Chinese intelligence. Those allegations have not been established in court. Nvidia's board retained the law firm Wachtell , Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether Huang had been the target of a foreign-intelligence effort. The board said it had no reason to believe that national security or Nvidia's proprietary information had been compromised. The available reporting does not establish a causal link between any specific allegation and Huang's resignation. Huang's exit could reduce Nvidia's influence in Washington at a moment when chip-export policy remains unsettled. Huang had become an influential figure in U.S. AI policy debates, advocating on chip-export rules and open-source AI access. He maintained a close public relationship with President Trump; that relationship included a May trip to China and an August appearance where Trump joined an AI discussion by telephone, according to CNBC. His departure may reduce Nvidia's near-term political reach, though that outcome remains uncertain while the board works through succession. Several consequential questions about Nvidia's future will not be answered by Tuesday's announcement alone. Who becomes permanent CEO, and does Kress retain the CFO role throughout a search that could last months? What will the board's investigation ultimately conclude, and will any findings require further public disclosure? Whether Nvidia revisits its China strategy and export-control posture under new leadership, or holds the course Huang set, may prove the most significant long-term question of all. What is confirmed: Huang is out, Kress leads on an interim basis, a formal search is underway, and Nvidia's board has pledged that operations and the product roadmap will continue without interruption.

passages: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .

Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. extraction.body: By LIA ZHU in San Francisco | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-11-13 11:22 Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy. Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman. Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion. The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily. "Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power. He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations. The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership. The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China. Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled. US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China. Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift. "AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report. Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed. The report said major US technology companies depend on Chinese companies in their supply chains, while American startups benefit from research published by Chinese companies, students and independent researchers using those chips. "The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning," the analysts wrote. Regarding supply chain, Gibbs said, Nvidia's ties with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and other partners in Taiwan are deeply institutional and unlikely to be disrupted by a leadership change. Instead, he expects closer scrutiny of distributors and data center operators in Southeast Asia, alongside tighter enforcement against the diversion of chips to China. "For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said. "Under interim leadership and intense scrutiny from the FBI and Congress, I would expect Nvidia to become far more cautious." That could mean less lobbying against export controls, tighter oversight of distributors and a lower public profile on China, he said. The regulatory pressure will also shape the challenges facing Kress and whoever succeeds her. Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy.

Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement.

The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman.
Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion.

The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily.

"Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power.
He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations.

The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership.
The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China.

Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China.
Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift.
"AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report.

Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed.

The report said major US technology companies depend on Chinese companies in their supply chains, while American startups benefit from research published by Chinese companies, students and independent researchers using those chips.
"The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning," the analysts wrote.
Regarding supply chain, Gibbs said, Nvidia's ties with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and other partners in Taiwan are deeply institutional and unlikely to be disrupted by a leadership change.
Instead, he expects closer scrutiny of distributors and data center operators in Southeast Asia, alongside tighter enforcement against the diversion of chips to China.

"For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said. "Under interim leadership and intense scrutiny from the FBI and Congress, I would expect Nvidia to become far more cautious."
That could mean less lobbying against export controls, tighter oversight of distributors and a lower public profile on China, he said.

The regulatory pressure will also shape the challenges facing Kress and whoever succeeds her. Gibbs said he would watch next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation, the selection of a permanent chief executive, the findings of investigations and any changes to export controls.
"The biggest challenge for the interim CEO, and her eventual successor, will be rebuilding trust with regulators," he said.

For startups, dependence on Nvidia rests primarily on its products and software ecosystem, which are continuing through the transition, Gibbs said. However, Nvidia could slow its strategic investments under interim leadership, while investors may scrutinize startups with exposure to China or Southeast Asian data center operators more closely.
Huang's departure also removes a business leader with unusual access to the White House, potentially changing the balance of voices influencing US technology policy.

High-profile executives have long provided an additional channel of communication between the US and China, Gibbs said, although their commercial responsibilities differ from those of officials charged with national security.
"He was also an important voice that ran counter to the national security hawks. His absence will certainly shift that balance," he said.

For companies operating across the two countries, the episode highlights the need for governance and institutional relationships that can withstand pressure, Gibbs said. Personal access can become a vulnerability when business spans countries engaged in strategic competition.
Even so, he said Huang's departure would not necessarily undermine Nvidia's competitiveness.

"He's been the sole face of the company externally, but there are a lot of smart and capable people who have a hand in running a company like Nvidia," Gibbs said. "It's hard to imagine Nvidia collapsing without him."

As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son. On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said. Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times. Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer." "I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC. That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks. Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
passages: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.
