Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. extraction.body: By LIA ZHU in San Francisco | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-11-13 11:22 Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy. Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman. Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion. The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily. "Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power. He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations. The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership. The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China. Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled. US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China. Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift. "AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report. Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed. The report said major US technology companies depend on Chinese companies in their supply chains, while American startups benefit from research published by Chinese companies, students and independent researchers using those chips. "The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning," the analysts wrote. Regarding supply chain, Gibbs said, Nvidia's ties with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and other partners in Taiwan are deeply institutional and unlikely to be disrupted by a leadership change. Instead, he expects closer scrutiny of distributors and data center operators in Southeast Asia, alongside tighter enforcement against the diversion of chips to China. "For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said. "Under interim leadership and intense scrutiny from the FBI and Congress, I would expect Nvidia to become far more cautious." That could mean less lobbying against export controls, tighter oversight of distributors and a lower public profile on China, he said. The regulatory pressure will also shape the challenges facing Kress and whoever succeeds her. Gibbs said he would watch next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation, the selection of a permanent chief executive, the findings of investigations and any changes to export controls. "The biggest challenge for the interim CEO, and her eventual successor, will be rebuilding trust with regulators," he said. For startups, dependence on Nvidia rests primarily on its products and software ecosystem, which are continuing through the transition, Gibbs said. However, Nvidia could slow its strategic investments under interim leadership, while investors may scrutinize startups with exposure to China or Southeast Asian data center operators more closely. Huang's departure also removes a business leader with unusual access to the White House, potentially changing the balance of voices influencing US technology policy. High-profile executives have long provided an additional channel of communication between the US and China, Gibbs said, although their commercial responsibilities differ from those of officials charged with national security. "He was also an important voice that ran counter to the national security hawks. His absence will certainly shift that balance," he said. For companies operating across the two countries, the episode highlights the need for governance and institutional relationships that can withstand pressure, Gibbs said. Personal access can become a vulnerability when business spans countries engaged in strategic competition. Even so, he said Huang's departure would not necessarily undermine Nvidia's competitiveness. "He's been the sole face of the company externally, but there are a lot of smart and capable people who have a hand in running a company like Nvidia," Gibbs said. "It's hard to imagine Nvidia collapsing without him."

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned following revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis. The 63-year-old will be replaced by chief financial officer Colette Kress, who will serve as interim chief executive. His exit comes after he admitted to having a relationship with a woman that US authorities believe was a Chinese spy. It also emerged on Wednesday that Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive. Nvidia shares were down more than 10 percent in pre-market trading, extending earlier losses after the announcement of Huang’s resignation. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, led it to become what was until recently the world’s most valuable company. Huang’s departure marks a startling end to his more than 33-year tenure, during which Nvidia evolved from a small video-game chip company into the linchpin of the global AI infrastructure boom. Huang has become one of the most recognizable figures in tech, as Nvidia’s semiconductors became integral to training and running AI systems such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. Nvidia stock extended its pre-market decline after the company announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive. Shares were down 10.2 percent in pre-market trading, a move that would wipe off more than $400 billion in market capitalization. sources.title: Smart glasses are 'an invasion of privacy' - Meta's are selling better than ever - BBC
passages: Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.

Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent.

After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits.
In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made.

Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces".
"Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said.

Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns.
"They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year.
Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology.
Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up.
People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses.
The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online.

The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online. They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal. One woman told the BBC that when she asked the person who posted a secret recording of her to remove it, she was told that doing so was "a paid service". Meta's glasses are currently the most popular on the market, estimated to make up more than 80% of all AI or smart glasses sales, as the company was the first major tech player to launch such a product in recent years. Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information. People can start recording video or take a photo with a casual touch of the frames. The nature of the camera in Meta's glasses can be so unobtrusive that even their wearers have been caught off guard by what and when they're recording, and where those recordings are going. After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits. In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made. In the other, they said they did not know their videos were being shared by the company for review. Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. Today, seven million pairs and counting have been sold, according to the company. "They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year. Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology. Now, other major tech companies are planning to get in on what may have the potential to be the tech industry's long-awaited new product category. Apple is reportedly developing its own version of smart glasses, possibly to be released next year. Snap has said it will release a new version of its smart glasses, called Specs, this year. Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns. All are expected to offer some combination of artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) technology, as Meta's glasses do, which typically requires a camera. The way people may use the coming wave of smart glasses will not be all bad, of course. Mark Smith wears his Meta Ray-Bans every day. "I've used them around the world, in all kinds of places. The basic features are great," Smith said. As a partner at the advisory firm ISG where he focuses on enterprise software, Smith can be classified as a tech-savvy early adopter. But the reasons he likes the glasses are not about any huge leaps in technological capability. He likes to wear them while washing up the dishes at home because they make it easy for him to listen to music or a podcast without blocking out other noise like most headphones do. Taking phone calls through the glasses is a breeze. When travelling, it's nice not to have to constantly pull out his phone to snap a quick picture or video. Even so, Smith said some potential privacy issues are obvious. The small light that turns on when the glasses are recording appears dim in daylight and often goes unnoticed, he said. Most people seem to have no idea he's wearing anything other than normal eyeglasses. Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years. If such a prediction becomes reality, the ability of institutions to enforce norms and laws that typically prohibit recording in places like courthouses, museums, movie theatres, hospitals and bathrooms will be difficult when suddenly millions of eyeglasses are also cameras. David Kessler, an attorney who heads the US privacy practice at Norton Rose Fulbright, said many of his corporate clients are already having to grapple with this. "There are some pretty dark places we could go here," Kessler said. "I'm not anti-technology in any sense, but as a societal matter...will I need to think [of being recorded] anytime I go out in public?" And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well. Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces". An increasingly popular use of the glasses is to record pranks on unsuspecting people. Wearers, often young men, get people to sign fake petitions or retail workers to smell candles sprayed with bad odours. Sometimes they steal food as it's being handed over at a drive-thru and record their sprint. People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses. Online influencer Aniessa Navarro said she felt sick when she realised during a personal waxing session that her technician was wearing Meta's glasses. The technician said they weren't charged or recording, and that she needed to wear them for the prescription lenses. Andrew Bosworth, Meta's chief technology officer, was asked on Instagram two weeks ago about "the stigma around people wearing smart glasses every day". He responded by saying that the sheer number of Meta Ray-Bans sold "suggest that these are widely accepted". But David Harris, a former Meta AI researcher who now teaches at UC Berkeley and is an adviser on AI policy in the US and EU, said he expects this generation of AI smart glasses to run up against the same issues that doomed the Google Glass more than a decade ago. "Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said. More signs of such a backlash are starting to appear.

passages: Bystanders told Google during years of research that they worried about being filmed without their knowledge, and that a sign of recording would help them most.
Wearers face a different exposure, because glasses that see what they see also capture menus, street signs, and the faces of strangers.
Before using the glasses, wearers must agree not to record people without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the light.
Google may disable the glasses of anyone who breaks those terms, and setup requires an 18+ Google Account.
Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here!
Google Shopping and Ads policies ban promoting products that disable or hide recording lights on smart glasses.
When the wearer asks Gemini about the scene, the glasses are designed to redact bystanders’ faces before Gemini processes the image.
Google keeps those camera visuals out of the user’s Gemini History and out of AI training and ad targeting.
The tamper detection, the face redaction, and the voice focus are design intentions.
Private AI Compute, Google’s hardened environment for processing data, has not reached the glasses yet.
Test the first three before you allow the glasses into a room with sensitive material on display.
Google has built its Gemini-powered intelligent eyewear to stop taking photos and video when someone covers or tampers with the outward-facing recording light.
Shahram Izadi, Google’s VP and GM of XR, laid out that safeguard along with face redaction, limits on data handling, and app restrictions.

extraction.body: Cybersecurity research and insight for the AI era · Moving soon to the ESET Blog Cybersecurity research and insight for the AI era · Moving soon to the ESET Blog Smart glasses allow anyone to track and record the world around them. That could put your data and the privacy of those nearby at risk. Fashion and many other trends have a way of reappearing every few years. So we probably shouldn’t be surprised that smart glasses are doing the rounds once more, after a failed attempt by Google to popularize them over a decade ago. The difference this time round is that they’re not just more stylish – and arguably harder to tell from regular shades. They’re also packed with far more powerful technology, capable of tracking and recording their surroundings, and allowing the user to ask AI about the things they can see around them. This presents significant security and privacy risks for both smart glasses users and the people they interact with. Anyone who’s ever lived in a city will be used to being monitored. Germany and the UK have among the highest number of CCTV cameras in the world. But when that monitoring is targeted and not based around informed consent, it can quickly get out of hand. Smart glasses give anyone the ability to record or take photos of strangers surreptitiously. Although they feature a small LED light, this can be covered up, and in any case may be difficult for bystanders to spot. But that’s not all. Harvard University researchers have demonstrated how video taken via smart glasses and livestreamed to Instagram can be connected to AI. Algorithms then work to identify faces and then pull information from the internet on those individuals. Suddenly that cool accessory becomes a powerful, portable surveillance device capable of empowering stalkers , bullies and fraudsters . This isn’t just about privacy. Any sensitive information shared with a public AI platform via a pair of smart glasses could theoretically be regurgitated to other users if prompted in the right way. That’s a potential security risk if they choose to use the information fraudulently. And then there are those outsourced workers and contractors who may stumble across information harvested by glasses, which they might decide to sell to scammers. Information you might accidentally send to the cloud/AI model could include: There’s also a risk of nefarious smart glasses users shoulder surfing behind you in public, in order to steal PINs, passwords and other secrets. Combined with facial recognition technology , this data extraction may allow them to build up a sizeable digital profile on their targets. With enough detail they could either launch convincing phishing attacks, hijack your accounts or impersonate you in new account creation attempts. Like any smart device, glasses could also be hacked more conventionally, by: These attack vectors could in turn enable bad actors to hijack your device for direct data theft, account takeover, or surveillance that could put you in physical danger. Whether you are wearing them or being observed by someone else, there are a few steps you can take to mitigate the risks we’ve outlined above: Meta isn’t the only tech giant rolling out smart glasses. Google, Apple, Amazon and a host of Chinese players are said to be developing similar products. Unfortunately, many prioritize competitive advantage over users’ rights. extraction.body: Sam Taylor shows off his AI glasses inside his office at Vision Australia in Brisbane. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) AI smart glasses are proving transformative for blind or low-vision users, helping them identify objects, read labels and improve their independence. The smart glasses have emerged as a significantly cheaper alternative to traditional assistive eyewear. Researchers and legal experts warn smart glasses are also enabling covert surveillance, and Australian legislation has not caught up. Thanks to a set of glasses, Sam Taylor no longer has to pull out his phone at the fridge, open an app, and point the camera in the right direction. "Daily I go and check the mail, and now it's easier than ever to identify and separate junk mail from things I might want to keep." Sam Taylor says the smart glasses allow users "to perform a plethora of additional options". ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) For members of the blind and low-vision community, AI-powered glasses are proving invaluable. Wollongong-based folk singer Sam Noonan has been blind since birth. After a demonstration of the glasses at a Vision Australia Expo, she "bought them on the spot". She has used her smart glasses to record and upload her music online, and to describe the drawings her grandchildren bring home from school. Meta Glasses mean more independence for Sam Noonan. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) While they were not designed as an accessibility device, Mr Taylor said the glasses were an alternative to traditional assistive eyewear, which typically costs about $5,000. "What we're seeing here is a device, which is a tenth of that cost, that allows us not only to read things out loud, but to perform a plethora of additional options," he said. The glasses can play music, read documents and call friends. Sam Noonan has used the smart glasses, and Meta's AI assistant, to re-categorise her wardrobe by colour and formality. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) As an access technology lead at Vision Australia, Mr Taylor believed the glasses' biggest advantage was not what they could do, but how naturally people could use them. "The uptake has been pretty amazing," he said. A key feature of the glasses is their integration with the app Be My Eyes, which allows users to call sighted volunteers. The volunteers can then see through the point of view of the lenses and assist with everyday tasks. Through his glasses, Mr Taylor used Be My Eyes to help with travel. Sam Taylor uses smart glasses with the Be My Eyes app to help him travel independently. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) But as the uptake of smart glasses increases, researchers and legal experts warn about increased privacy risks. Milica Stilinovic is an emerging technology researcher at the University of Sydney. Dr Stilinovic said the glasses could be used as a covert surveillance device, including the emerging genre of men filming themselves picking up women. Milica Stilinovic says the inconspicuous lens on the glasses can mean people are unaware they are being filmed. ( Supplied: Milica Stilinovic ) Dr Stilinovic said the inconspicuous camera meant subjects were unaware they were being filmed until the footage was published online. Barbara McDonald says prosecution for privacy breaches is difficult. ( Supplied: Barbara McDonald ) University of Sydney law expert Barbara McDonald said using smart glasses to record a private conversation and also publish it was in breach of the NSW Surveillance Devices Act. "Once you post something onto the internet … you might be in breach of the Federal Crimes Act or the Telecommunications Act, particularly if you were using that footage or those photographs to harass or intimidate somebody," Professor McDonald said. Last year, the Australian parliament introduced a new statutory tort enabling individuals to sue for serious invasions of privacy. Professor McDonald said while the tort offered an individual better privacy protection, prosecution was difficult. "If, of course, they can find the perpetrator, and if the perpetrator is in the jurisdiction, and all those sorts of procedural issues and costs," she said.

coreStoryFacts.text: Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.

Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent.

After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits.
In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made.

Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces".
"Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said.

Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns.
"They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year.
Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology.
Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up.
People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses.
The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online.
They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal.

And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well.

Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information.
Bystanders told Google during years of research that they worried about being filmed without their knowledge, and that a sign of recording would help them most.
Wearers face a different exposure, because glasses that see what they see also capture menus, street signs, and the faces of strangers.
Before using the glasses, wearers must agree not to record people without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the light.
Google may disable the glasses of anyone who breaks those terms, and setup requires an 18+ Google Account.

Google Shopping and Ads policies ban promoting products that disable or hide recording lights on smart glasses.
When the wearer asks Gemini about the scene, the glasses are designed to redact bystanders’ faces before Gemini processes the image.
Google keeps those camera visuals out of the user’s Gemini History and out of AI training and ad targeting.
The tamper detection, the face redaction, and the voice focus are design intentions.

extraction.body: Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up. Yet some of the biggest technology companies in the world are poised to sell many millions of pairs in the coming years. Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent. The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online. They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal. One woman told the BBC that when she asked the person who posted a secret recording of her to remove it, she was told that doing so was "a paid service". Meta's glasses are currently the most popular on the market, estimated to make up more than 80% of all AI or smart glasses sales, as the company was the first major tech player to launch such a product in recent years. Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information. People can start recording video or take a photo with a casual touch of the frames. The nature of the camera in Meta's glasses can be so unobtrusive that even their wearers have been caught off guard by what and when they're recording, and where those recordings are going. After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits. In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made. In the other, they said they did not know their videos were being shared by the company for review. Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. Today, seven million pairs and counting have been sold, according to the company. "They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year. Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology. Now, other major tech companies are planning to get in on what may have the potential to be the tech industry's long-awaited new product category. Apple is reportedly developing its own version of smart glasses, possibly to be released next year. Snap has said it will release a new version of its smart glasses, called Specs, this year. Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns. All are expected to offer some combination of artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) technology, as Meta's glasses do, which typically requires a camera. The way people may use the coming wave of smart glasses will not be all bad, of course. Mark Smith wears his Meta Ray-Bans every day. "I've used them around the world, in all kinds of places. The basic features are great," Smith said. As a partner at the advisory firm ISG where he focuses on enterprise software, Smith can be classified as a tech-savvy early adopter. But the reasons he likes the glasses are not about any huge leaps in technological capability. He likes to wear them while washing up the dishes at home because they make it easy for him to listen to music or a podcast without blocking out other noise like most headphones do. Taking phone calls through the glasses is a breeze. When travelling, it's nice not to have to constantly pull out his phone to snap a quick picture or video. Even so, Smith said some potential privacy issues are obvious. The small light that turns on when the glasses are recording appears dim in daylight and often goes unnoticed, he said. Most people seem to have no idea he's wearing anything other than normal eyeglasses. Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years. If such a prediction becomes reality, the ability of institutions to enforce norms and laws that typically prohibit recording in places like courthouses, museums, movie theatres, hospitals and bathrooms will be difficult when suddenly millions of eyeglasses are also cameras. David Kessler, an attorney who heads the US privacy practice at Norton Rose Fulbright, said many of his corporate clients are already having to grapple with this. "There are some pretty dark places we could go here," Kessler said. "I'm not anti-technology in any sense, but as a societal matter...will I need to think [of being recorded] anytime I go out in public?" And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well. Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces". An increasingly popular use of the glasses is to record pranks on unsuspecting people. Wearers, often young men, get people to sign fake petitions or retail workers to smell candles sprayed with bad odours. Sometimes they steal food as it's being handed over at a drive-thru and record their sprint. People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses. Online influencer Aniessa Navarro said she felt sick when she realised during a personal waxing session that her technician was wearing Meta's glasses. The technician said they weren't charged or recording, and that she needed to wear them for the prescription lenses. Andrew Bosworth, Meta's chief technology officer, was asked on Instagram two weeks ago about "the stigma around people wearing smart glasses every day". He responded by saying that the sheer number of Meta Ray-Bans sold "suggest that these are widely accepted". But David Harris, a former Meta AI researcher who now teaches at UC Berkeley and is an adviser on AI policy in the US and EU, said he expects this generation of AI smart glasses to run up against the same issues that doomed the Google Glass more than a decade ago. "Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said. More signs of such a backlash are starting to appear.

extraction.body: Sam Taylor shows off his AI glasses inside his office at Vision Australia in Brisbane. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) AI smart glasses are proving transformative for blind or low-vision users, helping them identify objects, read labels and improve their independence. The smart glasses have emerged as a significantly cheaper alternative to traditional assistive eyewear. Researchers and legal experts warn smart glasses are also enabling covert surveillance, and Australian legislation has not caught up. Thanks to a set of glasses, Sam Taylor no longer has to pull out his phone at the fridge, open an app, and point the camera in the right direction. "Daily I go and check the mail, and now it's easier than ever to identify and separate junk mail from things I might want to keep." Sam Taylor says the smart glasses allow users "to perform a plethora of additional options". ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) For members of the blind and low-vision community, AI-powered glasses are proving invaluable. Wollongong-based folk singer Sam Noonan has been blind since birth. After a demonstration of the glasses at a Vision Australia Expo, she "bought them on the spot". She has used her smart glasses to record and upload her music online, and to describe the drawings her grandchildren bring home from school. Meta Glasses mean more independence for Sam Noonan. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) While they were not designed as an accessibility device, Mr Taylor said the glasses were an alternative to traditional assistive eyewear, which typically costs about $5,000. "What we're seeing here is a device, which is a tenth of that cost, that allows us not only to read things out loud, but to perform a plethora of additional options," he said. The glasses can play music, read documents and call friends. Sam Noonan has used the smart glasses, and Meta's AI assistant, to re-categorise her wardrobe by colour and formality. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) As an access technology lead at Vision Australia, Mr Taylor believed the glasses' biggest advantage was not what they could do, but how naturally people could use them. "The uptake has been pretty amazing," he said. A key feature of the glasses is their integration with the app Be My Eyes, which allows users to call sighted volunteers. The volunteers can then see through the point of view of the lenses and assist with everyday tasks. Through his glasses, Mr Taylor used Be My Eyes to help with travel. Sam Taylor uses smart glasses with the Be My Eyes app to help him travel independently. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) But as the uptake of smart glasses increases, researchers and legal experts warn about increased privacy risks. Milica Stilinovic is an emerging technology researcher at the University of Sydney. Dr Stilinovic said the glasses could be used as a covert surveillance device, including the emerging genre of men filming themselves picking up women. Milica Stilinovic says the inconspicuous lens on the glasses can mean people are unaware they are being filmed. ( Supplied: Milica Stilinovic ) Dr Stilinovic said the inconspicuous camera meant subjects were unaware they were being filmed until the footage was published online. Barbara McDonald says prosecution for privacy breaches is difficult. ( Supplied: Barbara McDonald ) University of Sydney law expert Barbara McDonald said using smart glasses to record a private conversation and also publish it was in breach of the NSW Surveillance Devices Act. "Once you post something onto the internet … you might be in breach of the Federal Crimes Act or the Telecommunications Act, particularly if you were using that footage or those photographs to harass or intimidate somebody," Professor McDonald said. Last year, the Australian parliament introduced a new statutory tort enabling individuals to sue for serious invasions of privacy. Professor McDonald said while the tort offered an individual better privacy protection, prosecution was difficult. "If, of course, they can find the perpetrator, and if the perpetrator is in the jurisdiction, and all those sorts of procedural issues and costs," she said.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump has weighed in on Jensen Huang's resignation. Trump said former Apple CEO Tim Cook is the "only one man" to replace the Nvidia CEO. Trump has long praised Cook, once saying he was the only CEO in his first term who called him regularly on the phone. President Donald Trump has his own recommendation for Nvidia's next CEO — Tim Cook. In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump called Cook, Apple's former CEO, the "only one man" to replace Jensen Huang after the more-than-three-decade Nvidia boss resigned . "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump said in the post. Trump is a longtime fan of Cook, who stepped down as Apple's CEO earlier this year and took on the role of executive chairman of Apple's board of directors. The president has previously called Cook an "amazing manager and leader" and commended him for calling him directly on the phone . "He calls me and the others don't," Trump said during his first term. "Others go out and hire very expensive consultants, and Tim Cook calls Donald Trump directly. Pretty good." In April, after Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO, Trump called Cook an "incredible guy" in a Truth Social post. Trump added that Cook "had an AMAZING career, almost incomparable, and will go on and continue to do great work for Apple, and whatever else he chooses to work on." Nvidia's board of directors announced Huang's exit as the AI chip giant's CEO earlier Thursday, after a tumultuous week for Huang, marked by a company investigation and revelations about two extramarital affairs . On Sunday, Huang said in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years. "My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." This followed a New York Times report last month that said Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The report said US intelligence officials believe the woman was recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. The Nvidia founder's admission of an affair triggered an independent board investigation into the billionaire businessman. Amid that investigation, led by an elite Wall Street law firm , the Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Powell was one of Jensen Huang's direct reports. Nvidia said CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

WASHINGTON — President Trump floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook as a possible successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia Thursday — hours after Huang resigned as CEO of the leading artificial intelligence technology company following the exposure of extramarital affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG , who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

The leadership change comes at a time when Nvidia chips have become essential to the development of generative AI.
The firm is now at the centre of the US-China rivalry for dominance in artificial intelligence.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said Thursday that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress ahead of Thanksgiving.

sources.title: Microsoft Outlook is still down

extraction.body: Since just before 1PM ET on Thursday, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft quickly acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but not to the same extent, while Microsoft’s official updates said customers may experience issues across its suite of 365 business services. Microsoft comms director Ben Hope said in a statement that “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online. We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.” Several hours later, Microsoft has gone through several variations of update notes regarding the issues and its attempts to fix them, saying it’s had problems rebooting servers and being able to monitor their health. As of about 6PM ET, Microsoft has a note saying it’s managed to get some of the affected servers running: > We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions. > We’ve streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service. To further support recovery, we’re implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we’ll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results. As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service.

extraction.body: Since just before 1PM ET on Thursday, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft quickly acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but not to the same extent, while Microsoft’s official updates said customers may experience issues across its suite of 365 business services. Microsoft comms director Ben Hope said in a statement that “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online. We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.” Several hours later, Microsoft has gone through several variations of update notes regarding the issues and its attempts to fix them, saying it’s had problems rebooting servers and being able to monitor their health. As of about 6PM ET, Microsoft has a note saying it’s managed to get some of the affected servers running: > We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions. > We’ve streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service. To further support recovery, we’re implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we’ll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results. As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. Nvidia’s board launched an independent probe after a classified U.S. memo alleged Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang Nvidia makes the processors that power large-scale artificial intelligence systems. U.S. export controls restrict the most advanced of those chips from reaching China, a country competing directly with the United States in AI development. Those rules reflect bipartisan concern that advanced AI processors could accelerate China’s military and surveillance capabilities, which is what transforms the following sequence of events from a corporate personnel matter into a national-security concern. Jensen Huang leads Nvidia; Alice Huang ran operations at a firm built on Nvidia’s technology. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since. Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors. She is not related to Jensen Huang. Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public. During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time. U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator. In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex. The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public. The New York Times reported that in late 2025, President Trump was informed about intelligence concerning Alice Huang’s alleged activities and her relationship with Jensen Huang. No publicly announced action was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The briefing was not disclosed until reporting on the broader story emerged in late October 2026. U.S. officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, though that assessment has not been independently verified. In spring 2026 , U.S. officials reportedly circulated a classified memo alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security , the country’s primary civilian intelligence agency. The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang . It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China. This is an intelligence assessment reported by news organizations citing unnamed officials; it is not an established legal or investigative finding. Such government restrictions on technology access echo broader debates over how authorities worldwide handle sensitive data, as seen when Europe restricts major cloud providers from handling sensitive public-sector information. A New York Times report in October 2026 brought the relationship and the investigation into public view. On October 29, 2026 , the New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact. A rapid sequence of corporate and political responses followed that disclosure. Three House committee chairmen asked Jensen Huang to appear before a closed-door session. The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026. The letter cited concerns about Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology and possible infiltration of American technology companies. No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The CEO issued a public apology on November 8 without naming Alice Huang. On November 8, 2026 , Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged that he had been unfaithful, apologizing to his wife, children, Nvidia employees, and the company. He linked his statement to national-security concerns described in media coverage but did not identify Alice Huang by name. He also withdrew from planned appearances at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum. The board acted the following day, saying it had no immediate evidence of compromised secrets. On November 9, 2026 , Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason at that stage to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. President Trump said Jensen Huang should remain CEO. Trump later added that Huang had told him he did not know Alice Huang was allegedly a spy. Beijing’s Foreign Ministry called the espionage claim “groundless speculation.” On November 10, 2026 , China’s Foreign Ministry characterized the allegation that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence as a smear and rejected it as unsubstantiated. Corporate records, as reported by media, separately identified her as a Megaspeed director from March to November 2023. The supplied reporting does not identify her current status or whereabouts. The investigation is ongoing, and several core questions have no public answers yet. Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred. Nvidia’s independent board investigation has not released findings. Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven. Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public.

During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time.
U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator.

In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex.
The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public.

The New York Times reported that in late 2025, President Trump was informed about intelligence concerning Alice Huang’s alleged activities and her relationship with Jensen Huang. No publicly announced action was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The briefing was not disclosed until reporting on the broader story emerged in late October 2026.
U.S. officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, though that assessment has not been independently verified.

In spring 2026 , U.S. officials reportedly circulated a classified memo alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security , the country’s primary civilian intelligence agency. The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang . It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China. This is an intelligence assessment reported by news organizations citing unnamed officials; it is not an established legal or investigative finding. Such government restrictions on technology access echo broader debates over how authorities worldwide handle sensitive data, as seen when Europe restricts major cloud providers from handling sensitive public-sector information.
A New York Times report in October 2026 brought the relationship and the investigation into public view.

On October 29, 2026 , the New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact. A rapid sequence of corporate and political responses followed that disclosure.
Three House committee chairmen asked Jensen Huang to appear before a closed-door session.

The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026. The letter cited concerns about Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology and possible infiltration of American technology companies. No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time.
The CEO issued a public apology on November 8 without naming Alice Huang.

On November 8, 2026 , Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged that he had been unfaithful, apologizing to his wife, children, Nvidia employees, and the company. He linked his statement to national-security concerns described in media coverage but did not identify Alice Huang by name. He also withdrew from planned appearances at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum.
The board acted the following day, saying it had no immediate evidence of compromised secrets.

On November 9, 2026 , Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Beijing’s Foreign Ministry called the espionage claim “groundless speculation.”

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. extraction.body: Those experiencing difficulties accessing Outlook on Thursday need to first establish whether it is an issue with Microsoft’s servers or with their own account. Microsoft uses its official status site and Microsoft 365 Admin Center for service health information. For more information about the Exchange Online incident, administrators should look for incident EX1550543.Here are three ways users can check the situation:Microsoft service status: Visit Microsoft 365 Service Health for official information about service disruptions and recovery updates.Downdetector: Check Outlook outage reports to see whether other users are reporting similar problems.Microsoft 365 Admin Center: Organisations can check incident EX1550543 for information about the Exchange Online connectivity issue.There is also an option of trying to access Outlook using another approach, such as toggling between the desktop version and the web version of Outlook. Checking the internet connection and restarting the application can also help in case the issue is related to the user's side.However, changing passwords and reinstalling Outlook or changing account settings will not solve an infrastructure problem.Those who are waiting to send important messages for work can use other methods of communication for the time being.Microsoft's efforts to bring the unavailable servers back online and stabilise its remaining infrastructure are central to resolving the disruption. Reuters reported that more than 130,000 Outlook-related problem reports had been recorded by 1:27 p.m. Eastern Time.AP also reported more than 46,000 complaints involving Microsoft 365 and approximately 3,000 reports concerning Microsoft Teams.The disruption was not limited to Outlook.
