extraction.body: The “Intelligent Eyewear” is a collaboration between the two tech companies, with Samsung providing its hardware expertise and Google handling much of the software platform. Smart glasses are just one part of Android XR—there are also mixed-reality headsets and glasses for more immersive experiences, like last year's Samsung Galaxy XR and the upcoming Xreal Aura. Eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are heavily involved in the new smart glasses, responsible for the design and fit, similar to how Meta tapped Ray-Ban for its competing—and market-leading—wearables. Google and Samsung are leveraging Warby Parker and Gentle Monster's brick-and-mortar presence and retail expertise, which lets people demo the glasses before buying them. (Kering Eyewear, which owns brands like Lindberg and Maui Jim, has also signed up to make glasses for Android XR in the future.) The first models are available for preorder now, with official sales starting on December 10. Warby Parker's frames start at $395 and come in three styles—Alden, Reid, and Wren—as optical or sunglasses, with various prescription, lens, and width options. Gentle Monster's glasses start at $449 and come in six designs, various colors, and tints, with prescription options for most frames. The glasses weigh around 41 grams (10 grams less than Meta's new Gen 3 glasses), have a nine-hour battery life, and include a charging case that can recharge the glasses up to seven times. A touch-sensitive temple piece lets you tap to activate the onboard Gemini assistant, or slide two fingers back and forth to control the volume of the audio coming out of the glasses' speaker. They are the first devices to support the “Hey Gemini” hotword, though you can use the well-known “Hey Google” hotword if you'd like. Still, the new spoken wake phrase distinguishes the glasses as Gemini's “optimal form,” according to Juston Payne, Google's senior director of product management for XR. “We felt that these are a Gemini-forward device,” Payne tells WIRED. You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.” Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices—Google Pixel phones, Samsung Galaxy phones, and iPhones—and only select models. You'll need a Pixel 7 or newer, Galaxy S or Z Fold running Samsung's One UI 9.0 or higher, and the iPhone 13 Pro or newer. A Google spokesperson tells WIRED the company will share more about how it plans to expand support to other phones in 2027 after launch. Since you'll be buying the glasses from an eyewear brand, they will be the customer-facing party to handle any problems you may have with the device or prescriptions. Google has already previewed Intelligent Eyewear glasses with displays built into the lenses—useful for showing navigation instructions or real-time captions for folks with hearing issues. However, they are not ready yet; Payne says they're currently being tested by “non-Googlers” and are still on the road map, though he didn't share a specific release window. As for plans to launch audio-only smart glasses, like Meta's recent Ray-Ban Audio, Warby Parker co-CEO Dave Gilboa tells WIRED, “There's a pretty robust pipeline of additional products.” What Can They Do? Smart glasses have been around for a few years, but they come in many forms. Unlike display smart glasses designed to plug into a laptop to mirror or extend your screen, or more immersive glasses like Meta's VR Glasses, which layer virtual experiences over the real world, Intelligent Eyewear is more akin to what Google pitched years ago with the original Google Glass. You can listen to music, take phone calls, and get audio navigation through Google Maps. Yes, you can snap photos and videos too, though Payne quickly notes that these glasses are designed more to have Gemini assist you throughout the day than to capture content. That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “Glasshole”). “We learned through Glass that you can make people uncomfortable if you're not clearly communicating,” Payne says. To that end, Google is announcing a series of policies and features alongside the glasses to assuage concerns. When you ask Gemini to look at something, those visuals are not saved in your Gemini History, and Google says it will not use them to train AI models or target ads. The glasses will automatically redact the faces of people around you before Gemini processes the visual data. We've highlighted all of Google's privacy-focused announcements around its glasses in a separate story. Most of the features that Google is positioning around Intelligent Eyewear rely on Gemini. And if you use Samsung Notes on a Samsung phone, it'll know that's where you likely want your notes saved. A swipe back on the glasses' arm will end the interaction. Speaking of, early next year, Google says users can use gestures on devices like the Fitbit Air or Google Pixel Watch to control music playback or activate Gemini on the glasses right from their wrist. Google is also collaborating with Aira so you can stream the glasses' feed straight to a human interpreter for real-time visual support. To help demystify these features—and convince consumers that smart glasses aren't just a fad for tech bros—Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are both launching pop-up experiences in New York City this week. Gentle Monster's pop-up will run for about a month, but Warby Parker's “Literatureland” will be open through 2027, letting people walk through the experience with a pair of nonprescription glasses to demo Gemini's capabilities. “These are the original wearables that have been around for hundreds of years,” Warby Parker's Gilboa says.

extraction.body: The Xreal Aura, spatial computing glasses made in partnership with Google for the Android XR platform, are now available to order. We first learned about these XR glasses at Google I/O 2026, and early adopters can finally try them in a matter of weeks. The futuristic XR device combines elements of augmented reality and virtual reality in a pair of smart glasses. They're the first wired smart glasses to run on the new Android XR operating system from Google. The glasses and accessories are available for preorder at the Xreal website as of today, and they're scheduled to ship in mid-November, according to a press release shared with Mashable. Customers who preorder the glasses can save $180 on the hefty $1,279 price tag.“Xreal Aura is finally here, and we're so proud to unlock new ways for people to work, watch, play, and build," said Chi Xu, co-founder and CEO of XREAL, in a press release.The Xreal Aura utilizes dual Sony Micro-OLED displays to create a virtual display with a 70-degree field of view, up to 1,050 nits of brightness, and up to a 120Hz refresh rate. Credit: Xreal Credit: Xreal Xreal is one of the leading augmented reality companies, known for its tethered AR glasses, which project a large virtual display into the user's field of view. The Xreal Aura will provide spatial computing and virtual reality experiences usually associated with headsets in the smart glasses form factor.The Xreal Aura is part of a new generation of spatial computing smart glasses, along with the Specs AR glasses from Snap and the recently announced Meta VR glasses. The Meta VR glasses have a $1,299 price tag but won't launch until spring 2027.What do the Xreal Aura Glasses do? Credit: Xreal / Mashable Photo Composite Xreal says the new glasses will support "productivity, immersive entertainment, and next-generation XR experiences."The Xreal Aura offer the same augmented reality features as other AR smart glasses, but they up the ante with spatial computing experiences powered by the Android XR operating system and Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform. (A press release states that the glasses were made in partnership with Google and Qualcomm.) Unlike most AR glasses, the Xreal Aura can also be controlled via voice and hand movements, thanks to onboard sensors and cameras. Instead of simply plugging into a user's smartphone, laptop, or gaming device, the Aura glasses come with a puck, which houses the battery and powers most of the compute necessary for spatial computing.The Apple Vision Pro introduced spatial computing into the public consciousness. The technology turns a user's surroundings into a 360-degree virtual canvas, and users can open apps, games, entertainment, and AI tools directly into their space. However, unlike headsets, which can be extremely limiting, smart glasses don't limit a user's movements or block their peripheral vision. “This is a defining moment for XR," Xu said in a press release. "We built AURA for people who want the power of spatial computing without being removed from the world around them. With transparent lenses, a category-leading lightweight design, Gemini by your side, and access to the Android ecosystem from day-one, the promise of XR is more approachable than ever."The Xreal Aura will also offer support for Gemini, letting users ask questions about their environment or complete tasks across apps.Spatial photos, virtual reality, and more Credit: Xreal / Android XR Using Google Photos and Android XR, Aura users will be able to view their photos and videos in new immersive ways. Via Google Maps, users can explore destinations in immersive 3D, either with an aerial view or via Street View.Users can also enjoy 360-degree and VR180 video content on YouTube.New XR experiencesAt launch, users will also be able to access a library of more than 150 XR experiences, with more to come in the months ahead. Some of the highlights include:NBA App for Android XRFallout: Factions video gameProject Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, a mixed-reality adventure NASCAR XR appOh My Galaxy!, a physics-based arcade gameXR HoloMedicineSimply Piano XRWhere to preorder the Xreal AuraThe Xreal Aura are available for preorder now exclusively at the Xreal online store. The glasses have a retail price of $1,279 but are available for $1,099 for a limited time.

facts.text: Google I/O is less than a day away, and the annual software showcase would be the perfect opportunity for Google and its partners to showcase their 2026 Android XR tech: the XR glasses we’ve been promised will land this year.

Jensen Huang's "I made it" moment never translated to long weekends and a step back from day-to-day operations. Despite Nvidia becoming the world's most valuable company, its CEO Huang just admitted he still operates on a mix of fear, anxiety, and even going bankrupt. "You know the phrase '30 days from going out of business,' I've used for 33 years," Huang said on an episode of The Joe Rogan Experienc e . "But the feeling doesn't change. The sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity—it doesn't leave you." Nvidia has made itself one of the clear leaders in the AI race. What started as a graphics card producer grew into a tech powerhouse, building chips, systems, and software that power most large AI models in cloud data centers around the world. Last month, Nvidia became the first public company to reach a market capitalization of $5 trillion . Yet Huang still can't shake the feeling that the company could vanish overnight. "It is exhausting," he said, while adding that he's "always in a state of anxiety." The veteran CEO revealed he still works seven days a week, every moment he is awake to ensure his nightmare doesn't become—including checking his emails from 4 a.m.: "Every day. Every single day. Not one day missed. Including Thanksgiving, Christmas." Huang recounted an incident of a near collapse in the mid-1990s, when the company realized its first graphics technology was flawed just as it was developing a chip for Sega's next game console. With money running out, he flew to Japan to tell Sega's CEO the product wouldn't work and that they should cancel the deal, yet he also admitted Nvidia needed the final $5 million payment to stay afloat. Sega converted the remaining funds into an investment, giving the struggling startup the lifeline it needed to stay alive. "Suffering is part of the journey. You will appreciate it for these horrible feelings that you have when things are not going so well. You will appreciate it so much more when they do go well," he added. Huang previously wished Stanford students " ample doses of pain and suffering ". In his eyes, adversity is key to having resilience, low expectations and ultimately success. Even now, the fear of failure is still Huang's greatest motivator. "I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed," he said on the podcast. "Failure drives me more than greed or whatever it is." Huang isn't the only one to be born with the "work gene" in his family. Both of his kids work every day, too. Madison and Spencer, both in their 30s, started the company as interns in 2020 and 2022. "My kids work every day. Both of my kids work at Nvidia. They work every day," Huang said. Before that, both didn't show much interest in working for the company after high school. Madison attended the Culinary Institute of America , with her brother Spencer studying marketing in Chicago, then moving to Taiwan to study Mandarin, while doing so, he opened up a cocktail bar in Taipei. "Now we have three people working every day and they want to work with me every day and so it's a lot of work," Huang said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Jensen Huang's "I made it" moment never translated to long weekends and a step back from day-to-day operations. Despite Nvidia becoming the world's most valuable company, its CEO Huang just admitted he still operates on a mix of fear, anxiety, and even going bankrupt.

"You know the phrase '30 days from going out of business,' I've used for 33 years," Huang said on an episode of The Joe Rogan Experienc e . "But the feeling doesn't change. The sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity—it doesn't leave you."

Nvidia has made itself one of the clear leaders in the AI race. What started as a graphics card producer grew into a tech powerhouse, building chips, systems, and software that power most large AI models in cloud data centers around the world. Last month, Nvidia became the first public company to reach a market capitalization of $5 trillion . Yet Huang still can't shake the feeling that the company could vanish overnight.
"It is exhausting," he said, while adding that he's "always in a state of anxiety."

The veteran CEO revealed he still works seven days a week, every moment he is awake to ensure his nightmare doesn't become—including checking his emails from 4 a.m.: "Every day. Every single day. Not one day missed. Including Thanksgiving, Christmas."
Huang recounted an incident of a near collapse in the mid-1990s, when the company realized its first graphics technology was flawed just as it was developing a chip for Sega's next game console.

With money running out, he flew to Japan to tell Sega's CEO the product wouldn't work and that they should cancel the deal, yet he also admitted Nvidia needed the final $5 million payment to stay afloat. Sega converted the remaining funds into an investment, giving the struggling startup the lifeline it needed to stay alive.

"Suffering is part of the journey. You will appreciate it for these horrible feelings that you have when things are not going so well. You will appreciate it so much more when they do go well," he added.
Huang previously wished Stanford students " ample doses of pain and suffering ". In his eyes, adversity is key to having resilience, low expectations and ultimately success.
Even now, the fear of failure is still Huang's greatest motivator.
"I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed," he said on the podcast. "Failure drives me more than greed or whatever it is."
Huang isn't the only one to be born with the "work gene" in his family. Both of his kids work every day, too. Madison and Spencer, both in their 30s, started the company as interns in 2020 and 2022.
"My kids work every day. Both of my kids work at Nvidia. They work every day," Huang said.

Before that, both didn't show much interest in working for the company after high school. Madison attended the Culinary Institute of America , with her brother Spencer studying marketing in Chicago, then moving to Taiwan to study Mandarin, while doing so, he opened up a cocktail bar in Taipei.
"Now we have three people working every day and they want to work with me every day and so it's a lot of work," Huang said.
This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

sources.title: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI - CNBC
passages: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch.
During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience.
Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.
When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters.

While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it.
That approach persisted, as recently as this week.
Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks.
It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications.
The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012.

That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.
In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping .

Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley.
"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday.
"How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."
Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S.

He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term.
Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.
"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair.
"This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail.
I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG.
That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia.

She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China.

Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer."
"I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC.
Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering.
In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects.
That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.
Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

passages: The situation surrounding Huang has unfolded quickly, with The New York Times only reporting on Friday that Huang and the suspected spy were “close” before other dominoes started to fall, leading to a swift fall from grace for one of the biggest names in technology. (Hours after Huang’s resignation was announced, Reuters reported that he also had an “intimate relationship” with another Nvidia employee.) Prominent voices in technology have come out in support of Huang, with some calling the resignation a “waste” and a sad day for “all humanity.” The narrative among those leaders on X, at least, is that Huang’s resignation was rushed — perhaps an overreaction to salacious news stories about his personal life.
Nvidia announced this morning that Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO following reports of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report.
Some others have had a more neutral reaction, commenting more on Huang’s achievements at the company’s helm.

extraction.body: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake. On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government. But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go. The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list. Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him? Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed , writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built. It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign. Erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote . “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.” U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang. Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.” Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat. For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. passages: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake.

On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government.
But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go.

The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list.
Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him?

Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed , writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built.
It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.

Erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote . “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.”

U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang.

Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.”

Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat.

For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform.

That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.”

Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them.
The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services.

Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.”

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance , which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions.

The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang.
OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban.

The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.
That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence —arguably, the most powerful company on earth.

Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote , praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company.

Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote . He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI.

Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X . “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.”
If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.

Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.”

Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy.
In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts.

Bitcoin and privacy advocate Neil Woodfine described Huang as a founder who had built Nvidia to the pinnacle and championed free, local AI, only to be displaced by a managerial establishment convinced it could do better.

This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern…
— Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026

Not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit , warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. The concern from Washington has been largely uniform: the possibility of compromising pressure against the leader of a company central to U.S. AI infrastructure.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has remained supportive of Huang: “He’s definitely suffering,” he told the press. “I think he’ll be in good shape.”
Speculation about Huang’s next job spread just as quickly as criticism of his last one. Responding to an X user asking him to hire Huang, Elon Musk replied , “That would be an honor.”

Jensen Huang's "I made it" moment never translated to long weekends and a step back from day-to-day operations. Despite Nvidia becoming the world's most valuable company, its CEO Huang just admitted he still operates on a mix of fear, anxiety, and even going bankrupt.

"You know the phrase '30 days from going out of business,' I've used for 33 years," Huang said on an episode of The Joe Rogan Experienc e . "But the feeling doesn't change. The sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity—it doesn't leave you."

Nvidia has made itself one of the clear leaders in the AI race. What started as a graphics card producer grew into a tech powerhouse, building chips, systems, and software that power most large AI models in cloud data centers around the world. Last month, Nvidia became the first public company to reach a market capitalization of $5 trillion . Yet Huang still can't shake the feeling that the company could vanish overnight.
"It is exhausting," he said, while adding that he's "always in a state of anxiety."

The veteran CEO revealed he still works seven days a week, every moment he is awake to ensure his nightmare doesn't become—including checking his emails from 4 a.m.: "Every day. Every single day. Not one day missed. Including Thanksgiving, Christmas."
Huang recounted an incident of a near collapse in the mid-1990s, when the company realized its first graphics technology was flawed just as it was developing a chip for Sega's next game console.

With money running out, he flew to Japan to tell Sega's CEO the product wouldn't work and that they should cancel the deal, yet he also admitted Nvidia needed the final $5 million payment to stay afloat. Sega converted the remaining funds into an investment, giving the struggling startup the lifeline it needed to stay alive.

"Suffering is part of the journey. You will appreciate it for these horrible feelings that you have when things are not going so well. You will appreciate it so much more when they do go well," he added.
Huang previously wished Stanford students " ample doses of pain and suffering ". In his eyes, adversity is key to having resilience, low expectations and ultimately success.
Even now, the fear of failure is still Huang's greatest motivator.
"I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed," he said on the podcast. "Failure drives me more than greed or whatever it is."
Huang isn't the only one to be born with the "work gene" in his family. Both of his kids work every day, too. Madison and Spencer, both in their 30s, started the company as interns in 2020 and 2022.
"My kids work every day. Both of my kids work at Nvidia. They work every day," Huang said.

Before that, both didn't show much interest in working for the company after high school. Madison attended the Culinary Institute of America , with her brother Spencer studying marketing in Chicago, then moving to Taiwan to study Mandarin, while doing so, he opened up a cocktail bar in Taipei.
"Now we have three people working every day and they want to work with me every day and so it's a lot of work," Huang said.
This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

extraction.body: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake. On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government. But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go. The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list. Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him? Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed , writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built. It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign. Erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote . “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.” U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang. Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.” Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat. For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform. That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.” Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them. The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services. Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.” In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance , which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions. The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang. OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban. The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027. That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence —arguably, the most powerful company on earth. Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote , praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company. Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote . He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI. Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X . “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.” If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right. passages: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake.

On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government.
But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go.

The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list.
Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him?

Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed , writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built.
It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.

Erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote . “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.”

U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang.

Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote . “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.”

Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat.

For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked , alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform.

That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.”

Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them.
The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services.

Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.”

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance , which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions.

The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang.
OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban.

The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.
That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence —arguably, the most powerful company on earth.

Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote , praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company.

Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote . He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI.

Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X . “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.”
If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.

Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy.
In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts.

Bitcoin and privacy advocate Neil Woodfine described Huang as a founder who had built Nvidia to the pinnacle and championed free, local AI, only to be displaced by a managerial establishment convinced it could do better.

Not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit , warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. passages: Even so, he said Huang's departure would not necessarily undermine Nvidia's competitiveness.

Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy.
Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement.
The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees.
The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman.
For startups, dependence on Nvidia rests primarily on its products and software ecosystem, which are continuing through the transition, Gibbs said.
However, Nvidia could slow its strategic investments under interim leadership, while investors may scrutinize startups with exposure to China or Southeast Asian data center operators more closely.
"For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said.
Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion.
The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week.
The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership.
The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China.
"It's hard to imagine Nvidia collapsing without him."
Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised.
House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled.
"The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models.

extraction.body: By LIA ZHU in San Francisco | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-11-13 11:22 Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy. Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman. Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion. The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily. "Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power. He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations. The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership. The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China. Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled. US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China. Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift. "AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report. Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed. The report said major US technology companies depend on Chinese companies in their supply chains, while American startups benefit from research published by Chinese companies, students and independent researchers using those chips. "The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning," the analysts wrote. Regarding supply chain, Gibbs said, Nvidia's ties with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and other partners in Taiwan are deeply institutional and unlikely to be disrupted by a leadership change. Instead, he expects closer scrutiny of distributors and data center operators in Southeast Asia, alongside tighter enforcement against the diversion of chips to China. "For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said. "Under interim leadership and intense scrutiny from the FBI and Congress, I would expect Nvidia to become far more cautious." That could mean less lobbying against export controls, tighter oversight of distributors and a lower public profile on China, he said. The regulatory pressure will also shape the challenges facing Kress and whoever succeeds her. Gibbs said he would watch next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation, the selection of a permanent chief executive, the findings of investigations and any changes to export controls. "The biggest challenge for the interim CEO, and her eventual successor, will be rebuilding trust with regulators," he said. For startups, dependence on Nvidia rests primarily on its products and software ecosystem, which are continuing through the transition, Gibbs said. However, Nvidia could slow its strategic investments under interim leadership, while investors may scrutinize startups with exposure to China or Southeast Asian data center operators more closely. Huang's departure also removes a business leader with unusual access to the White House, potentially changing the balance of voices influencing US technology policy. High-profile executives have long provided an additional channel of communication between the US and China, Gibbs said, although their commercial responsibilities differ from those of officials charged with national security. "He was also an important voice that ran counter to the national security hawks. His absence will certainly shift that balance," he said. For companies operating across the two countries, the episode highlights the need for governance and institutional relationships that can withstand pressure, Gibbs said. Personal access can become a vulnerability when business spans countries engaged in strategic competition. Even so, he said Huang's departure would not necessarily undermine Nvidia's competitiveness. "He's been the sole face of the company externally, but there are a lot of smart and capable people who have a hand in running a company like Nvidia," Gibbs said. "It's hard to imagine Nvidia collapsing without him."

Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy.

Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement.

The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman.
Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion.

The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily.

"Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power.
He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations.

The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership.
The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China.

Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China.
Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift.
"AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report.

Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed.

The report said major US technology companies depend on Chinese companies in their supply chains, while American startups benefit from research published by Chinese companies, students and independent researchers using those chips.
"The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning," the analysts wrote.
Regarding supply chain, Gibbs said, Nvidia's ties with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and other partners in Taiwan are deeply institutional and unlikely to be disrupted by a leadership change.
Instead, he expects closer scrutiny of distributors and data center operators in Southeast Asia, alongside tighter enforcement against the diversion of chips to China.

"For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said. "Under interim leadership and intense scrutiny from the FBI and Congress, I would expect Nvidia to become far more cautious."
That could mean less lobbying against export controls, tighter oversight of distributors and a lower public profile on China, he said.

The regulatory pressure will also shape the challenges facing Kress and whoever succeeds her. Gibbs said he would watch next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation, the selection of a permanent chief executive, the findings of investigations and any changes to export controls.
"The biggest challenge for the interim CEO, and her eventual successor, will be rebuilding trust with regulators," he said.

For startups, dependence on Nvidia rests primarily on its products and software ecosystem, which are continuing through the transition, Gibbs said. However, Nvidia could slow its strategic investments under interim leadership, while investors may scrutinize startups with exposure to China or Southeast Asian data center operators more closely.
Huang's departure also removes a business leader with unusual access to the White House, potentially changing the balance of voices influencing US technology policy.

High-profile executives have long provided an additional channel of communication between the US and China, Gibbs said, although their commercial responsibilities differ from those of officials charged with national security.
"He was also an important voice that ran counter to the national security hawks. His absence will certainly shift that balance," he said.

For companies operating across the two countries, the episode highlights the need for governance and institutional relationships that can withstand pressure, Gibbs said. Personal access can become a vulnerability when business spans countries engaged in strategic competition.
Even so, he said Huang's departure would not necessarily undermine Nvidia's competitiveness.

"He's been the sole face of the company externally, but there are a lot of smart and capable people who have a hand in running a company like Nvidia," Gibbs said. "It's hard to imagine Nvidia collapsing without him."

coreStoryFacts.text: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch.
During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience.
Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.
When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters.

While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it.
That approach persisted, as recently as this week.
Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks.
It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications.
The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012.

That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.
In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping .

Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley.
"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday.
"How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."
Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S.
