extraction.body: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market." When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it. One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated. Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son. On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said. Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times. Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer." "I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC. That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks. Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. extraction.body: By LIA ZHU in San Francisco | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-11-13 11:22 Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on Thursday, four days after admitting to an extramarital affair, leaving the chipmaker facing a leadership transition and raising questions about the direction of the AI industry and US chip export policy. Nvidia's board announced that Huang, the company's co-founder, had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice-president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. The departure followed media reports alleging three extramarital affairs, including two involving Nvidia employees. The other woman, whom Huang admitted to having an affair with, was a Chinese businesswoman. Following the news, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14 percent before recovering most of their losses to close 4.3 percent lower at $166.19, leaving the company with a market value of $4.01 trillion. The leadership change has created uncertainty for a company central to the AI industry, but its immediate implications may be more limited than the initial market reaction suggested, Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told China Daily. "Jensen Huang played an important role in maintaining customer relationships, but demand for Nvidia's products remains strong, and his departure doesn't change that," said Gibbs, author of The Fragile Dragon: China's Strengths and the Limits to its Power. He said the stock was down about 30 percent from its October peak, although much of the decline preceded the scandal and reflected broader concerns about AI valuations. The reaction so far has largely been specific to Nvidia, Gibbs said, noting that the broader market and other chip stocks rose this week. The forces driving AI development are diverse and well-funded, he added, and do not depend on one company's leadership. The more consequential change could emerge in Washington, where Huang had been a prominent advocate against tight restrictions on chip sales to China. Lawmakers have called for investigations into whether national security was compromised. House Republicans were discussing possible congressional testimony with Huang sometime this month, The New York Times reported, although no appearance has been scheduled. US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting semiconductor chip exports to China. Analysts at SemiAnalysis, a Silicon Valley AI research firm, said Huang's departure could accelerate that shift. "AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone," Dylan Patel and three other analysts wrote in a report. Patel, the firm's founder and chief executive, warned that poorly shaped restrictions could damage US interests by disrupting supply chains and weakening the development of open-source AI models, which Huang had championed. The report said major US technology companies depend on Chinese companies in their supply chains, while American startups benefit from research published by Chinese companies, students and independent researchers using those chips. "The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning," the analysts wrote. Regarding supply chain, Gibbs said, Nvidia's ties with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and other partners in Taiwan are deeply institutional and unlikely to be disrupted by a leadership change. Instead, he expects closer scrutiny of distributors and data center operators in Southeast Asia, alongside tighter enforcement against the diversion of chips to China. "For Nvidia specifically, the company has lost its most effective advocate for access to the Chinese market," Gibbs said. "Under interim leadership and intense scrutiny from the FBI and Congress, I would expect Nvidia to become far more cautious." That could mean less lobbying against export controls, tighter oversight of distributors and a lower public profile on China, he said. The regulatory pressure will also shape the challenges facing Kress and whoever succeeds her. Gibbs said he would watch next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation, the selection of a permanent chief executive, the findings of investigations and any changes to export controls. "The biggest challenge for the interim CEO, and her eventual successor, will be rebuilding trust with regulators," he said. For startups, dependence on Nvidia rests primarily on its products and software ecosystem, which are continuing through the transition, Gibbs said. However, Nvidia could slow its strategic investments under interim leadership, while investors may scrutinize startups with exposure to China or Southeast Asian data center operators more closely. Huang's departure also removes a business leader with unusual access to the White House, potentially changing the balance of voices influencing US technology policy. High-profile executives have long provided an additional channel of communication between the US and China, Gibbs said, although their commercial responsibilities differ from those of officials charged with national security. "He was also an important voice that ran counter to the national security hawks. His absence will certainly shift that balance," he said. For companies operating across the two countries, the episode highlights the need for governance and institutional relationships that can withstand pressure, Gibbs said. Personal access can become a vulnerability when business spans countries engaged in strategic competition. Even so, he said Huang's departure would not necessarily undermine Nvidia's competitiveness. "He's been the sole face of the company externally, but there are a lot of smart and capable people who have a hand in running a company like Nvidia," Gibbs said. "It's hard to imagine Nvidia collapsing without him."

Nvidia now faces a question that confronts any company whose identity is closely tied to one leader: How much of what made the company successful should its next CEO preserve, and what should that person have the freedom to change? These six articles from the HBR archive look at how boards can make that judgment, choose a successor, and help that person take charge. Leading After the Founder Samantha Hellauer, Sanja Kos, Julie Vermoote, Sapna Sadarangani Werner, and BJ Wright (January-February 2026) A founder’s departure can unsettle a company in ways an ordinary CEO transition rarely does. Successors can earn credibility by learning why certain practices took hold and deciding which ones will serve the company in its next phase. . . . Beware the Transition from an Iconic CEO Elena Lytkina Botelho, Shoma Hayden, and BJ Wright (February 2023) Disney’s return to Bob Iger and Starbucks’s repeated handoffs from Howard Schultz illustrate how hard it can be for a successor to emerge from the shadow of a celebrated CEO. . . . Choose the Right CEO for Volatile Times Claudius A. Hildebrand, Kate Hurley, and Giovanna Galli (September-October 2025) Drawing on research into CEO transitions at major U.S. and European companies, the authors make the case for looking at the range of situations a candidate has handled, including organizational change, failure, and recovery. . . . extraction.body: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday, November 12, after reports about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, interim CEO and appointed Harvey C. Huang had led Nvidia since cofounding it in 1993. Nvidia now faces a question that confronts any company whose identity is closely tied to one leader: How much of what made the company successful should its next CEO preserve, and what should that person have the freedom to change? These six articles from the HBR archive look at how boards can make that judgment, choose a successor, and help that person take charge. Leading After the Founder Samantha Hellauer, Sanja Kos, Julie Vermoote, Sapna Sadarangani Werner, and BJ Wright (January-February 2026) A founder’s departure can unsettle a company in ways an ordinary CEO transition rarely does. Successors can earn credibility by learning why certain practices took hold and deciding which ones will serve the company in its next phase. . . . Beware the Transition from an Iconic CEO Elena Lytkina Botelho, Shoma Hayden, and BJ Wright (February 2023) Disney’s return to Bob Iger and Starbucks’s repeated handoffs from Howard Schultz illustrate how hard it can be for a successor to emerge from the shadow of a celebrated CEO. . . . Choose the Right CEO for Volatile Times Claudius A. Hildebrand, Kate Hurley, and Giovanna Galli (September-October 2025) Drawing on research into CEO transitions at major U.S. and European companies, the authors make the case for looking at the range of situations a candidate has handled, including organizational change, failure, and recovery. . . . Power, Influence, and CEO Succession Dan Ciampa and Adam Bryant (July-August 2024) Ciampa and Bryant examine the shifting relationships among directors, the outgoing chief, and the incoming leader, and explain how those dynamics can help a successor take charge or undermine that person’s ability to lead. . . . This legitimacy will be gained by consistently demonstrating specific behaviors. . . . What New CEOs Should Ask Themselves in Their First 100 Days by Paul Griggs and Paul Leinwand (August 2025) Questions to help you build a strong foundation of trust, alignment, and enthusiasm.

sources.title: Smart glasses are 'an invasion of privacy' - Meta's are selling better than ever - BBC
passages: Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.

Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent.

After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits.
In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made.

Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces".
"Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said.

Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns.
"They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year.
Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology.
Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up.
People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses.
The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online.
They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal.

And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well.

Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information.
Wearers, often young men, get people to sign fake petitions or retail workers to smell candles sprayed with bad odours.

extraction.body: Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up. Yet some of the biggest technology companies in the world are poised to sell many millions of pairs in the coming years. Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent. The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online. They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal. One woman told the BBC that when she asked the person who posted a secret recording of her to remove it, she was told that doing so was "a paid service". Meta's glasses are currently the most popular on the market, estimated to make up more than 80% of all AI or smart glasses sales, as the company was the first major tech player to launch such a product in recent years. Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information. People can start recording video or take a photo with a casual touch of the frames. The nature of the camera in Meta's glasses can be so unobtrusive that even their wearers have been caught off guard by what and when they're recording, and where those recordings are going. After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits. In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made. In the other, they said they did not know their videos were being shared by the company for review. Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. Today, seven million pairs and counting have been sold, according to the company. "They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year. Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology. Now, other major tech companies are planning to get in on what may have the potential to be the tech industry's long-awaited new product category. Apple is reportedly developing its own version of smart glasses, possibly to be released next year. Snap has said it will release a new version of its smart glasses, called Specs, this year. Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns. All are expected to offer some combination of artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) technology, as Meta's glasses do, which typically requires a camera. The way people may use the coming wave of smart glasses will not be all bad, of course. Mark Smith wears his Meta Ray-Bans every day. "I've used them around the world, in all kinds of places. The basic features are great," Smith said. As a partner at the advisory firm ISG where he focuses on enterprise software, Smith can be classified as a tech-savvy early adopter. But the reasons he likes the glasses are not about any huge leaps in technological capability. He likes to wear them while washing up the dishes at home because they make it easy for him to listen to music or a podcast without blocking out other noise like most headphones do. Taking phone calls through the glasses is a breeze. When travelling, it's nice not to have to constantly pull out his phone to snap a quick picture or video. Even so, Smith said some potential privacy issues are obvious. The small light that turns on when the glasses are recording appears dim in daylight and often goes unnoticed, he said. Most people seem to have no idea he's wearing anything other than normal eyeglasses. Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years. If such a prediction becomes reality, the ability of institutions to enforce norms and laws that typically prohibit recording in places like courthouses, museums, movie theatres, hospitals and bathrooms will be difficult when suddenly millions of eyeglasses are also cameras. David Kessler, an attorney who heads the US privacy practice at Norton Rose Fulbright, said many of his corporate clients are already having to grapple with this. "There are some pretty dark places we could go here," Kessler said. "I'm not anti-technology in any sense, but as a societal matter...will I need to think [of being recorded] anytime I go out in public?" And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well. Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces". An increasingly popular use of the glasses is to record pranks on unsuspecting people. Wearers, often young men, get people to sign fake petitions or retail workers to smell candles sprayed with bad odours. Sometimes they steal food as it's being handed over at a drive-thru and record their sprint. People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses. Online influencer Aniessa Navarro said she felt sick when she realised during a personal waxing session that her technician was wearing Meta's glasses. The technician said they weren't charged or recording, and that she needed to wear them for the prescription lenses. Andrew Bosworth, Meta's chief technology officer, was asked on Instagram two weeks ago about "the stigma around people wearing smart glasses every day". He responded by saying that the sheer number of Meta Ray-Bans sold "suggest that these are widely accepted". But David Harris, a former Meta AI researcher who now teaches at UC Berkeley and is an adviser on AI policy in the US and EU, said he expects this generation of AI smart glasses to run up against the same issues that doomed the Google Glass more than a decade ago. "Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said. More signs of such a backlash are starting to appear.

extraction.body: Sam Taylor shows off his AI glasses inside his office at Vision Australia in Brisbane. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) AI smart glasses are proving transformative for blind or low-vision users, helping them identify objects, read labels and improve their independence. The smart glasses have emerged as a significantly cheaper alternative to traditional assistive eyewear. Researchers and legal experts warn smart glasses are also enabling covert surveillance, and Australian legislation has not caught up. Thanks to a set of glasses, Sam Taylor no longer has to pull out his phone at the fridge, open an app, and point the camera in the right direction. "Daily I go and check the mail, and now it's easier than ever to identify and separate junk mail from things I might want to keep." Sam Taylor says the smart glasses allow users "to perform a plethora of additional options". ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) For members of the blind and low-vision community, AI-powered glasses are proving invaluable. Wollongong-based folk singer Sam Noonan has been blind since birth. After a demonstration of the glasses at a Vision Australia Expo, she "bought them on the spot". She has used her smart glasses to record and upload her music online, and to describe the drawings her grandchildren bring home from school. Meta Glasses mean more independence for Sam Noonan. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) While they were not designed as an accessibility device, Mr Taylor said the glasses were an alternative to traditional assistive eyewear, which typically costs about $5,000. "What we're seeing here is a device, which is a tenth of that cost, that allows us not only to read things out loud, but to perform a plethora of additional options," he said. The glasses can play music, read documents and call friends. Sam Noonan has used the smart glasses, and Meta's AI assistant, to re-categorise her wardrobe by colour and formality. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) As an access technology lead at Vision Australia, Mr Taylor believed the glasses' biggest advantage was not what they could do, but how naturally people could use them. "The uptake has been pretty amazing," he said. A key feature of the glasses is their integration with the app Be My Eyes, which allows users to call sighted volunteers. The volunteers can then see through the point of view of the lenses and assist with everyday tasks. Through his glasses, Mr Taylor used Be My Eyes to help with travel. Sam Taylor uses smart glasses with the Be My Eyes app to help him travel independently. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) But as the uptake of smart glasses increases, researchers and legal experts warn about increased privacy risks. Milica Stilinovic is an emerging technology researcher at the University of Sydney. Dr Stilinovic said the glasses could be used as a covert surveillance device, including the emerging genre of men filming themselves picking up women. Milica Stilinovic says the inconspicuous lens on the glasses can mean people are unaware they are being filmed. ( Supplied: Milica Stilinovic ) Dr Stilinovic said the inconspicuous camera meant subjects were unaware they were being filmed until the footage was published online. Barbara McDonald says prosecution for privacy breaches is difficult. ( Supplied: Barbara McDonald ) University of Sydney law expert Barbara McDonald said using smart glasses to record a private conversation and also publish it was in breach of the NSW Surveillance Devices Act. "Once you post something onto the internet … you might be in breach of the Federal Crimes Act or the Telecommunications Act, particularly if you were using that footage or those photographs to harass or intimidate somebody," Professor McDonald said. Last year, the Australian parliament introduced a new statutory tort enabling individuals to sue for serious invasions of privacy. Professor McDonald said while the tort offered an individual better privacy protection, prosecution was difficult. "If, of course, they can find the perpetrator, and if the perpetrator is in the jurisdiction, and all those sorts of procedural issues and costs," she said.

coreStoryFacts.text: Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.

Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent.

After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits.
In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made.

Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces".
"Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said.

Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns.
"They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year.
Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology.
Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up.
People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses.
The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online.
They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal.

extraction.body: Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up. Yet some of the biggest technology companies in the world are poised to sell many millions of pairs in the coming years. Women leaving the beach , going into a shop, or simply standing outside are now being approached by men usually wearing Meta's Ray-Bans, the company's "smart" or "AI" glasses, often in order to film the women's responses to casual questions or pick-up lines without their knowledge or consent. The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online. They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal. One woman told the BBC that when she asked the person who posted a secret recording of her to remove it, she was told that doing so was "a paid service". Meta's glasses are currently the most popular on the market, estimated to make up more than 80% of all AI or smart glasses sales, as the company was the first major tech player to launch such a product in recent years. Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information. People can start recording video or take a photo with a casual touch of the frames. The nature of the camera in Meta's glasses can be so unobtrusive that even their wearers have been caught off guard by what and when they're recording, and where those recordings are going. After workers in Kenya, tasked with watching videos made through Meta's glasses to create AI training data for the company, said they were being required to watch graphic content like sex and bathroom usage , people who own the glasses filed two lawsuits. In one, people said they had no idea such videos had been made. In the other, they said they did not know their videos were being shared by the company for review. Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. Today, seven million pairs and counting have been sold, according to the company. "They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year. Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology. Now, other major tech companies are planning to get in on what may have the potential to be the tech industry's long-awaited new product category. Apple is reportedly developing its own version of smart glasses, possibly to be released next year. Snap has said it will release a new version of its smart glasses, called Specs, this year. Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns. All are expected to offer some combination of artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) technology, as Meta's glasses do, which typically requires a camera. The way people may use the coming wave of smart glasses will not be all bad, of course. Mark Smith wears his Meta Ray-Bans every day. "I've used them around the world, in all kinds of places. The basic features are great," Smith said. As a partner at the advisory firm ISG where he focuses on enterprise software, Smith can be classified as a tech-savvy early adopter. But the reasons he likes the glasses are not about any huge leaps in technological capability. He likes to wear them while washing up the dishes at home because they make it easy for him to listen to music or a podcast without blocking out other noise like most headphones do. Taking phone calls through the glasses is a breeze. When travelling, it's nice not to have to constantly pull out his phone to snap a quick picture or video. Even so, Smith said some potential privacy issues are obvious. The small light that turns on when the glasses are recording appears dim in daylight and often goes unnoticed, he said. Most people seem to have no idea he's wearing anything other than normal eyeglasses. Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years. If such a prediction becomes reality, the ability of institutions to enforce norms and laws that typically prohibit recording in places like courthouses, museums, movie theatres, hospitals and bathrooms will be difficult when suddenly millions of eyeglasses are also cameras. David Kessler, an attorney who heads the US privacy practice at Norton Rose Fulbright, said many of his corporate clients are already having to grapple with this. "There are some pretty dark places we could go here," Kessler said. "I'm not anti-technology in any sense, but as a societal matter...will I need to think [of being recorded] anytime I go out in public?" And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well. Meta markets its glasses under the tagline: "Designed for privacy, controlled by you." It suggests to users of the glasses that they do not record people who state they do not want to be recorded, and that users turn the glasses off completely "in sensitive spaces". An increasingly popular use of the glasses is to record pranks on unsuspecting people. Wearers, often young men, get people to sign fake petitions or retail workers to smell candles sprayed with bad odours. Sometimes they steal food as it's being handed over at a drive-thru and record their sprint. People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses. Online influencer Aniessa Navarro said she felt sick when she realised during a personal waxing session that her technician was wearing Meta's glasses. The technician said they weren't charged or recording, and that she needed to wear them for the prescription lenses. Andrew Bosworth, Meta's chief technology officer, was asked on Instagram two weeks ago about "the stigma around people wearing smart glasses every day". He responded by saying that the sheer number of Meta Ray-Bans sold "suggest that these are widely accepted". But David Harris, a former Meta AI researcher who now teaches at UC Berkeley and is an adviser on AI policy in the US and EU, said he expects this generation of AI smart glasses to run up against the same issues that doomed the Google Glass more than a decade ago. "Technology like this is fundamentally an invasion of privacy and it's really going to face more and more backlash," he said. More signs of such a backlash are starting to appear.

Google, too, is set to try again with smart glasses, more than a decade after its notorious Google Glass flop, which the company pulled from the public within two years of launch as the pricey gadget came under fire over privacy concerns.
"They're some of the fastest-growing consumer electronics in history," Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, boasted earlier this year.
Tracy Clayton, a Meta spokesman, told the BBC that people should behave responsibly with any technology.
Issues with a new wave of "smart glasses" seem to be piling up.
People do often recoil when they discover a person is wearing smart glasses.
The women only find out about the videos of them after they gain traction, and often abuse, online.
They have little legal recourse as photography in public is broadly considered legal.

And Meta reportedly plans to add facial recognition technology in an updated version of its glasses, meaning wearers could not only have the ability to surreptitiously record anyone, but quickly identify them, as well.

Made in partnership with EssilorLuxottica and offering the classic look of Ray-Bans, the glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, small speakers in the arms, and in the latest version lenses that can show a wearer some information.
Wearers, often young men, get people to sign fake petitions or retail workers to smell candles sprayed with bad odours.

extraction.body: Sam Taylor shows off his AI glasses inside his office at Vision Australia in Brisbane. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) AI smart glasses are proving transformative for blind or low-vision users, helping them identify objects, read labels and improve their independence. The smart glasses have emerged as a significantly cheaper alternative to traditional assistive eyewear. Researchers and legal experts warn smart glasses are also enabling covert surveillance, and Australian legislation has not caught up. Thanks to a set of glasses, Sam Taylor no longer has to pull out his phone at the fridge, open an app, and point the camera in the right direction. "Daily I go and check the mail, and now it's easier than ever to identify and separate junk mail from things I might want to keep." Sam Taylor says the smart glasses allow users "to perform a plethora of additional options". ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) For members of the blind and low-vision community, AI-powered glasses are proving invaluable. Wollongong-based folk singer Sam Noonan has been blind since birth. After a demonstration of the glasses at a Vision Australia Expo, she "bought them on the spot". She has used her smart glasses to record and upload her music online, and to describe the drawings her grandchildren bring home from school. Meta Glasses mean more independence for Sam Noonan. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) While they were not designed as an accessibility device, Mr Taylor said the glasses were an alternative to traditional assistive eyewear, which typically costs about $5,000. "What we're seeing here is a device, which is a tenth of that cost, that allows us not only to read things out loud, but to perform a plethora of additional options," he said. The glasses can play music, read documents and call friends. Sam Noonan has used the smart glasses, and Meta's AI assistant, to re-categorise her wardrobe by colour and formality. ( ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss ) As an access technology lead at Vision Australia, Mr Taylor believed the glasses' biggest advantage was not what they could do, but how naturally people could use them. "The uptake has been pretty amazing," he said. A key feature of the glasses is their integration with the app Be My Eyes, which allows users to call sighted volunteers. The volunteers can then see through the point of view of the lenses and assist with everyday tasks. Through his glasses, Mr Taylor used Be My Eyes to help with travel. Sam Taylor uses smart glasses with the Be My Eyes app to help him travel independently. ( ABC News: Paul Adam ) But as the uptake of smart glasses increases, researchers and legal experts warn about increased privacy risks. Milica Stilinovic is an emerging technology researcher at the University of Sydney. Dr Stilinovic said the glasses could be used as a covert surveillance device, including the emerging genre of men filming themselves picking up women. Milica Stilinovic says the inconspicuous lens on the glasses can mean people are unaware they are being filmed. ( Supplied: Milica Stilinovic ) Dr Stilinovic said the inconspicuous camera meant subjects were unaware they were being filmed until the footage was published online. Barbara McDonald says prosecution for privacy breaches is difficult. ( Supplied: Barbara McDonald ) University of Sydney law expert Barbara McDonald said using smart glasses to record a private conversation and also publish it was in breach of the NSW Surveillance Devices Act. "Once you post something onto the internet … you might be in breach of the Federal Crimes Act or the Telecommunications Act, particularly if you were using that footage or those photographs to harass or intimidate somebody," Professor McDonald said. Last year, the Australian parliament introduced a new statutory tort enabling individuals to sue for serious invasions of privacy. Professor McDonald said while the tort offered an individual better privacy protection, prosecution was difficult. "If, of course, they can find the perpetrator, and if the perpetrator is in the jurisdiction, and all those sorts of procedural issues and costs," she said.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump has weighed in on Jensen Huang's resignation. Trump said former Apple CEO Tim Cook is the "only one man" to replace the Nvidia CEO. Trump has long praised Cook, once saying he was the only CEO in his first term who called him regularly on the phone. President Donald Trump has his own recommendation for Nvidia's next CEO — Tim Cook. In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump called Cook, Apple's former CEO, the "only one man" to replace Jensen Huang after the more-than-three-decade Nvidia boss resigned . "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump said in the post. Trump is a longtime fan of Cook, who stepped down as Apple's CEO earlier this year and took on the role of executive chairman of Apple's board of directors. The president has previously called Cook an "amazing manager and leader" and commended him for calling him directly on the phone . "He calls me and the others don't," Trump said during his first term. "Others go out and hire very expensive consultants, and Tim Cook calls Donald Trump directly. Pretty good." In April, after Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO, Trump called Cook an "incredible guy" in a Truth Social post. Trump added that Cook "had an AMAZING career, almost incomparable, and will go on and continue to do great work for Apple, and whatever else he chooses to work on." Nvidia's board of directors announced Huang's exit as the AI chip giant's CEO earlier Thursday, after a tumultuous week for Huang, marked by a company investigation and revelations about two extramarital affairs . On Sunday, Huang said in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years. "My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." This followed a New York Times report last month that said Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The report said US intelligence officials believe the woman was recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. The Nvidia founder's admission of an affair triggered an independent board investigation into the billionaire businessman. Amid that investigation, led by an elite Wall Street law firm , the Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Powell was one of Jensen Huang's direct reports. Nvidia said CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. Trump has long praised Cook, once saying he was the only CEO in his first term who called him regularly on the phone. President Donald Trump has his own recommendation for Nvidia's next CEO — Tim Cook. In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump called Cook, Apple's former CEO, the "only one man" to replace Jensen Huang after the more-than-three-decade Nvidia boss resigned . "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump said in the post. Trump is a longtime fan of Cook, who stepped down as Apple's CEO earlier this year and took on the role of executive chairman of Apple's board of directors. The president has previously called Cook an "amazing manager and leader" and commended him for calling him directly on the phone . "He calls me and the others don't," Trump said during his first term. "Others go out and hire very expensive consultants, and Tim Cook calls Donald Trump directly. Pretty good." In April, after Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO, Trump called Cook an "incredible guy" in a Truth Social post. Trump added that Cook "had an AMAZING career, almost incomparable, and will go on and continue to do great work for Apple, and whatever else he chooses to work on." Nvidia's board of directors announced Huang's exit as the AI chip giant's CEO earlier Thursday, after a tumultuous week for Huang, marked by a company investigation and revelations about two extramarital affairs . On Sunday, Huang said in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years. "My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." This followed a New York Times report last month that said Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The report said US intelligence officials believe the woman was recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. The Nvidia founder's admission of an affair triggered an independent board investigation into the billionaire businessman. Amid that investigation, led by an elite Wall Street law firm , the Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Powell was one of Jensen Huang's direct reports. Nvidia said CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. Other large corporations have made similar announcements recently, including Bank of America, which cautioned users last week to never share user IDs and passwords with agents. Many companies, particularly banks and airlines, have faced mounting difficulty as they try to separate human customers from their AI assistants. The firms warn that consumers’ credentials are at risk of leaking when they entrust agents with their logins and passwords. “Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” United said in a Wednesday press release . Automated AI actions also could break Federal Aviation Administration and Department of Transportation rules, the release said, citing the fact that flight check-in requires “human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.” The airline is implementing the new access restrictions both within its own digital platforms and separately through aggregators and agencies. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies,” the press release said. United Airlines is stepping off the AI bandwagon. It's the first carrier to explicitly ban third-party AI bots from making bookings or upgrades. There are multiple reasons for this: Security and federal compliance are the obvious ones. But each query costs the airline money, and United doesn't want to pay for AI bot queries.

United Airlines is spooked by AI travel agents. The airline updated its contract to bar AI agents from making, changing, or servicing tickets and from buying seats, upgrades, or other products. This is even when the traveler supervises or approves each step.

United has the right to cancel such reservations without notice, and the ban reaches AI tools offered through travel agencies. AI agents can search and display fares, but the traveler must personally complete the booking. The airline is concerned that consumers sharing credentials with AI agents is an inherent security risk. And check-ins need to be done personally as per federal laws to declare that the bags carry no banned items.

The airline has read the pulse of the people on this one: A fraud-detection survey found 43% of Americans would let AI book with final approval, but only 12% would allow fully autonomous booking. Similar data from 2025 stated that over 40% of the respondents were not comfortable with letting AI plan their trips.

The real motive here is to avoid added costs, especially when fuel costs are eating airlines' lunch. AI bots from large metasearch engines can produce 100 billion inquiries a day and that costs airlines money. There are no accurate estimates for the cost but an Air France-KLM 2024 policy shows an excess fee of €0.70 per 1,000 queries once a seller passes a 1,000-to-1 search-to-booking baseline. So it's not much per search but it adds up, especially when AI agents make billions of queries a day.

It's only United that's implemented an outright ban. Meanwhile, other industry rivals are actively working with AI. Delta allows authenticated AI assistants to complete bookings, with added safeguards for sensitive trips such as unaccompanied minors. Southwest lets ChatGPT users browse its seats and find trips.

But across the board, companies are still sitting on the fence about AI. Amazon won a preliminary injunction against Perplexity's Comet agent in March. JPMorgan Chase blocks agents. Meanwhile, Walmart lets outside agents buy within customer-set limits such as $50 or $100.

Changing the rules is just the first step. Enforcing them is a lot harder. A contract ban cannot rule out purchases made by AI bots on online travel agents like Expedia. United would still see it as an Expedia booking.

Then there's the question of reciprocating the good faith by not using AI to influence fares. Airlines face their own AI scrutiny too. In October, the FTC ordered United, Delta, JetBlue, and six other carriers to disclose how they use AI for pricing fares. So this street goes both ways.

extraction.body: United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations. The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

extraction.body: United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations. The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

passages: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has now been accused of having an ‘intimate’ relationship with another employee at the company, bringing a third reported affair into light in the scandal that resulted in his resignation, said a Reuters report, citing two sources.
The latest revelation comes after reports of two other extramarital relationships involving the ex-Nvidia boss led to the loss of his job.
One was with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and former executive at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials suspect of having links to Chinese intelligence.
The other affair was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who worked under Huang.
Huang has also hired the law firm Paul Weiss as scrutiny around his personal relationships and Nvidia’s business dealings in China intensifies.
Nvidia said chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO while the board considers both internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
Nvidia board has appointed former Synopsys CEO and long-time Nvidia director Harvey Jones as its new chair.
The leadership change comes at a time when Nvidia chips have become essential to the development of generative AI.
The firm is now at the centre of the US-China rivalry for dominance in artificial intelligence.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said Thursday that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress ahead of Thanksgiving.

extraction.body: Since just before 1PM ET on Thursday, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. extraction.body: If you’ve been unable to log into Microsoft Outlook, the outage has affected thousands like you. Millions of users worldwide reported problems accessing Microsoft Outlook and other 365 products Thursday (Nov. 12) evening. Microsoft is reporting widespread service disruptions across multiple Microsoft 365 applications, leaving some users unable to access email, collaborate in Teams, or use other workplace tools. The outage on Nov. 12 is affecting several services that interact with Exchange Online, Microsoft’s email platform. As of 9:55 p.m., more than 36,852 services reported problems accessing Microsoft Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products on downdetector.com . Users may experience difficulty accessing their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop applications, and mobile connections. Email delivery may also be delayed. Other affected services include Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft To Do, SharePoint Online, Power BI and Microsoft Defender. Microsoft said some Copilot users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses through the web and desktop applications. Copilot features that rely on work data, including emails, calendars and files, may also be unavailable. In Microsoft Teams, features that depend on Exchange Online, including calendar access, meeting scheduling, and certain chat functions, may fail. However, core messaging and online meetings remain largely functional. The disruption is also affecting Microsoft 365 administrators, who may have difficulty loading certain pages in the admin center. Other impacted services include Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, and Microsoft 365 Education. Microsoft said the issue may affect users attempting to access services across affected regions. Microsoft said it is applying infrastructure capacity improvements to help support increased traffic in regions coming online. The company is monitoring the results of those changes and evaluating additional actions to improve service health across affected regions. Microsoft’s next scheduled update was set for Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, at 3 a.m. UTC, which is 10 p.m. EST. Users experiencing problems may continue to encounter intermittent service disruptions as Microsoft works to restore normal operations. Copyright 2026 by WDIV ClickOnDetroit - All rights reserved. Millions of users worldwide reported problems accessing Microsoft Outlook and other 365 products Thursday (Nov. 12) evening. Microsoft is reporting widespread service disruptions across multiple Microsoft 365 applications, leaving some users unable to access email, collaborate in Teams, or use other workplace tools. As of 9:55 p.m., more than 36,852 services reported problems accessing Microsoft Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products on downdetector.com . Users may experience difficulty accessing their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop applications, and mobile connections. Email delivery may also be delayed. Other affected services include Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft To Do, SharePoint Online, Power BI and Microsoft Defender. Copilot features that rely on work data, including emails, calendars and files, may also be unavailable. In Microsoft Teams, features that depend on Exchange Online, including calendar access, meeting scheduling, and certain chat functions, may fail. However, core messaging and online meetings remain largely functional. The disruption is also affecting Microsoft 365 administrators, who may have difficulty loading certain pages in the admin center. Other impacted services include Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, and Microsoft 365 Education. Microsoft said the issue may affect users attempting to access services across affected regions. Microsoft said it is applying infrastructure capacity improvements to help support increased traffic in regions coming online. extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. The resignation followed revelations that Huang reportedly had affairs with two women: an executive who reported to him and a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill reacted swiftly. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said, “It was the right thing to do. Now we have to get to the bottom of whether America's national security has been compromised.” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-LA, called it “a big and shocking development,” adding, “That's a very important company not only in the U.S. economy but for national security purposes.” Although the affair became public this week, the timeline of events described in published reports stretches back years. According to The Wall Street Journal, in 2023 Alice Huang created 'Megaspeed,' a company seeking to build data centers in Asia using Nvidia chips. In June 2024, Alice and Jensen Huang were photographed together in Taiwan, and again in May 2025. Later that year, The New York Times reported that federal investigators were looking into 'Megaspeed,' the potential export of chips to China, and the connection between the two. In December, President Trump agreed to let Nvidia export a less powerful chip to China in exchange for 25% of the sales going to the federal government. By 2026, suspicion was reportedly growing. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reportedly supervising the drafting of a classified memo warning of a personal relationship between the two. The report of the memo came shortly before Huang was a last-minute addition to Trump’s China trip in May, which included various other tech giants. This week, Huang confirmed the extramarital relationship for the first time, writing, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children.” Nvidia stock continued to tumble in the aftermath of the news and Huang’s resignation. Yahoo Finance reported the company had shed $490 billion in market value by the end of trading Thursday. Nvidia’s board of directors also said Thursday that the company’s current executive vice president and CFO has agreed to serve as interim CEO, and that the board will search for Huang’s replacement, considering both internal and external candidates.
